nodes.name: Discrete analytic function
nodes.statement: A function $f:\ZZ^2\longrightarrow\CC$ is said to be {\em discrete analytic} if \[ \forall (x,y)\in \ZZ^2,\qquad \dfrac{f(x+1,y+1)-f(x,y)}{1+i}=\dfrac{f(x+1,y)-f(x,y+1)}{1-i}.\]
nodes.statement_short: A lattice function is discrete analytic when its two diagonal difference quotients on every unit square agree.

nodes.name: Failure of the pointwise product: $z$, $z^2$, $z^3$
nodes.statement: For example, the functions $z:=x+iy$ and $z^2$ are discrete analytic in the sense of Definition \ref{maindef}, but $z^3$ is not.
nodes.statement_short: $z$ and $z^2$ are discrete analytic while $z^3$ is not, so pointwise products leave the class.

nodes.name: Isaacs' conjecture on monodiffric rational functions
nodes.statement: In \cite{MR0052526} R. Isaacs has posed a conjecture that {\em all monodiffric rational functions are polynomials.}
nodes.statement_short: Isaacs conjectured that every monodiffric rational function is in fact a polynomial.
conclusions: all monodiffric rational functions are polynomials.

nodes.name: Harman's non-polynomial monodiffric rational function
nodes.statement: This conjecture was disproved by C. Harman in \cite{MR0361111}, where an explicit example of a non-polynomial monodiffric function, rational in one quadrant, was constructed.
nodes.statement_short: Harman's explicit non-polynomial monodiffric function, rational in one quadrant, refutes Isaacs' conjecture.

nodes.name: The polynomials $x^{[n]}$
nodes.statement: In what follows, $\Omega$ stands for one of two sets: $\ZZ$ or $\ZZ_+$, and $x^{[n]}$ denotes the polynomial of degree $n$ defined by \[ x^{[n]}:=\prod_{j=0}^{n-1}(x-j)\] (if $n=0,$ $x^{[0]}:=1$).
nodes.section: Polynomials and rational functions on the set of integers
nodes.statement_short: Introduces the falling-factorial basis $x^{[n]}=\prod_{j=0}^{n-1}(x-j)$, with $x^{[0]}=1$.

nodes.name: Generating function of the $x^{[k]}$
nodes.statement: They have the generating function \[ (1+t)^x=\sum_{k=0}^x x^{[k]}\frac{t^k}{k!}, \]
nodes.section: Polynomials and rational functions on the set of integers
nodes.statement_short: $(1+t)^x$ is the generating function of the falling factorials $x^{[k]}$.

nodes.name: Difference operator $\delta$
nodes.statement: The linear {\em difference operator} $\delta$ on the space of functions $f:\Omega\longrightarrow\CC$ is defined by $$(\delta f)(x)=f(x+1)-f(x),\quad x\in\Omega.$$
nodes.section: Polynomials and rational functions on the set of integers

nodes.name: Finiteness of the series $\check f$
nodes.statement: Let $f:\ZZ_+\longrightarrow \CC$. Then, for every $x\in\ZZ_+$ the series $$\check f(x):=\sum_{n\in\ZZ_+}f(n)x^{[n]}$$ has a finite number of non zero terms.
nodes.section: Polynomials and rational functions on the set of integers
nodes.statement_short: For $f$ on $\ZZ_+$ the expansion $\check f(x)=\sum f(n)x^{[n]}$ has only finitely many nonzero terms.
conclusions: Then, for every $x\in\ZZ_+$ the series $$\check f(x):=\sum_{n\in\ZZ_+}f(n)x^{[n]}$$ has a finite number of non zero terms.

nodes.name: Proof of finiteness of $\check f$
nodes.statement: In view of \eqref{poly}, $$\forall x\in\ZZ_+,\,\,\forall n\in\ZZ_+,\qquad x<n\Longrightarrow x^{[n]}=0.$$ Therefore, for every $x\in\ZZ_+$ the series $\check f(x)$ contains at most $x+1$ non-zero terms.
nodes.section: Polynomials and rational functions on the set of integers
nodes.statement_short: Since $x^{[n]}=0$ for $n>x$, at most $x+1$ terms survive.

nodes.name: Existence and uniqueness of the discrete Fourier coefficients
nodes.statement: Let $f:\ZZ_+\longrightarrow \CC$. Then there exists a unique function $\hat f:\ZZ_+\longrightarrow \CC$ such that \[\forall x\in\ZZ_+,\qquad f(x)=\sum_{n\in\ZZ_+} \hat f(n)x^{[n]}.\] The function $\hat f(n)$ is given by \[\hat f(n)=\dfrac{(\delta^nf)(0)}{n!}.\]
nodes.section: Polynomials and rational functions on the set of integers
nodes.statement_short: Every $f$ on $\ZZ_+$ has a unique expansion in the $x^{[n]}$, with coefficients $(\delta^n f)(0)/n!$.
conclusions: Then there exists a unique function $\hat f:\ZZ_+\longrightarrow \CC$ such that \[\forall x\in\ZZ_+,\qquad f(x)=\sum_{n\in\ZZ_+} \hat f(n)x^{[n]}.\]
The function $\hat f(n)$ is given by \[\hat f(n)=\dfrac{(\delta^nf)(0)}{n!}.\]

nodes.name: Proof of the discrete Taylor expansion
nodes.statement: To show the uniqueness of $\hat f(n)$, assume that \eqref{tay} holds for some function $\hat f(n)$ and apply the identity \[\delta x^{[n]}=nx^{[n-1]}\] repeatedly to obtain \eqref{fou1}.\\ Next, let the function $\hat f(n)$ be defined by \eqref{fou1}. Then, according to Proposition \ref{tay1}, the series $$\tilde f(x):=\sum_{n\in\ZZ_+} \hat f(n)x^{[n]}$$ converges absolutely for every $x\in\ZZ_+$ and defines a function $\tilde f:\ZZ_+\longrightarrow\CC.$ Hence \eqref{fou1} holds with $\tilde f$ replacing $f$ and $$\forall n\in\ZZ_+,\qquad (\delta^nf)(0)=n! \hat f(n)=(\delta^n\tilde f)(0).$$ Now one can verify that \[\forall x\in\ZZ_+,\,\,\forall n\in\ZZ_+,\qquad (\delta^nf)(x)=(\delta^n\tilde f)(x) \] by induction on $x$: If $$ \forall n\in\ZZ_+, \qquad (\delta^nf)(x)=(\delta^n\tilde f)(x)$$ then \begin{multline*} \forall n\in\ZZ_+, \qquad (\delta^nf)(x+1)=(\delta^nf)(x)+(\delta^{n+1}f)(x)\\= (\delta^n\tilde f)(x)+(\delta^{n+1}\tilde f)(x) =(\delta^n\tilde f)(x+1).\end{multline*} It remains to set $n=0$ in \eqref{hu1} to obtain \eqref{tay}.
nodes.section: Polynomials and rational functions on the set of integers
nodes.statement_short: Uniqueness by repeatedly applying $\delta x^{[n]}=nx^{[n-1]}$; existence by induction on $x$ for the constructed $\tilde f$.

nodes.name: Difference identity $\delta x^{[n]}=nx^{[n-1]}$
nodes.section: Polynomials and rational functions on the set of integers

nodes.name: Fourier transform of $f:\ZZ_+\to\CC$
nodes.statement: Let $f:\ZZ_+\longrightarrow \CC$. Then the function $\hat f:\ZZ_+\longrightarrow\CC,$ defined by \eqref{fou1}, is said to be the Fourier transform of $f$.
nodes.section: Polynomials and rational functions on the set of integers

nodes.name: Polynomial function on $\ZZ$
nodes.statement: Suppose that a function $f:\ZZ\longrightarrow\CC$ is such that $$\forall x\in\ZZ,\qquad f(x)=p(x),$$ where $p(x)$ is a polynomial with complex coefficients. Then such a polynomial $p(x)$ is unique, and we shall call the function $f$ itself a polynomial. If $f(x)\not\equiv 0,$ the degree of $f(x)$ is the same as the degree of $p(x)$.
nodes.section: Polynomials and rational functions on the set of integers
nodes.statement_short: A function on $\ZZ$ agreeing with a (necessarily unique) complex polynomial is itself called a polynomial.
differentia: $$\forall x\in\ZZ,\qquad f(x)=p(x),$$ where $p(x)$ is a polynomial with complex coefficients

nodes.name: Finite support of $\hat f$ for polynomial $f$ on $\ZZ$
nodes.statement: Let $f:\ZZ\longrightarrow\CC$ be a polynomial, and let $\hat f :\ZZ_+\longrightarrow\CC$ be the Fourier transform of the restriction $f_{|_{\ZZ_+}}$. Then the function $\hat f$ has a finite support and $$\forall x\in\ZZ,\qquad f(x)=\sum_{n\in\ZZ_+}\hat f(n)x^{[n]}.$$
nodes.section: Polynomials and rational functions on the set of integers
nodes.statement_short: A polynomial on $\ZZ$ has finitely supported Fourier transform and equals its $x^{[n]}$-expansion on all of $\ZZ$.
assumptions: Let $f:\ZZ\longrightarrow\CC$ be a polynomial, and let $\hat f :\ZZ_+\longrightarrow\CC$ be the Fourier transform of the restriction $f_{|_{\ZZ_+}}$
conclusions: Then the function $\hat f$ has a finite support and $$\forall x\in\ZZ,\qquad f(x)=\sum_{n\in\ZZ_+}\hat f(n)x^{[n]}.$$

nodes.name: Proof of finite support for polynomials on $\ZZ$
nodes.statement: Note that $$\deg(\delta f)=\deg(f)-1$$ (if $f=\const,$ $\delta f=0$). Hence $$\forall n\in\ZZ_+,\qquad n>\deg(f)\Longrightarrow \delta^nf=0.$$ Since $$(\delta f)_{|_{\ZZ_+}}=\delta(f_{|_{\ZZ_+}}),$$ \eqref{fou1} implies that $$\forall n>\deg(f),\qquad \hat f(n)=0.$$ It follows that $$\sum_{n\in\ZZ_+}\hat f(n)x^{[n]}$$ is, in fact, a polynomial, which coincides with the polynomial $f(x)$ on $\ZZ_+$ and hence on $\ZZ$.
nodes.section: Polynomials and rational functions on the set of integers
nodes.statement_short: Degree drops under $\delta$, so $\hat f(n)=0$ beyond $\deg f$ and the expansion is a polynomial agreeing with $f$.

nodes.name: Discrete antiderivative of a polynomial
nodes.statement: Let $f:\ZZ\longrightarrow\CC$ be a polynomial. Then there exists a polynomial $g:\ZZ\longrightarrow\CC$ such that $f(x)\equiv (\delta g)(x).$ If $f(x)\not\equiv0$ then $\deg(g)=\deg(f)+1.$
nodes.section: Polynomials and rational functions on the set of integers
nodes.statement_short: Every polynomial on $\ZZ$ is $\delta g$ for a polynomial $g$ of degree one higher.
conclusions: Then there exists a polynomial $g:\ZZ\longrightarrow\CC$ such that $f(x)\equiv (\delta g)(x).$
If $f(x)\not\equiv0$ then $\deg(g)=\deg(f)+1.$

nodes.name: Proof of the discrete antiderivative
nodes.statement: By Proposition \ref{p01}, $$ f(x)=\sum_{n\in\ZZ_+}\hat f(n)x^{[n]},$$ where $\hat f:\ZZ_+\longrightarrow\CC$ is a function with finite support. Consider the polynomial $$g(x)=\sum_{n\in\ZZ_+}\dfrac{\hat{f}(n)}{n+1}x^{[n+1]},$$ then, in view of \eqref{hu2}, $$\forall x\in\ZZ,\qquad (\delta g)(x)=\sum_{n\in\ZZ_+}{\hat{f}(n)}x^{[n]}=f(x).$$
nodes.section: Polynomials and rational functions on the set of integers
nodes.statement_short: Construct $g$ by shifting the $x^{[n]}$-expansion up one index and dividing by $n+1$.

nodes.name: Rational function on $\ZZ_+$
nodes.statement: A function $f:\ZZ_+\longrightarrow \CC$ is said to be {\em rational} if there exist polynomials $p,q:\ZZ_+\longrightarrow\CC$ such that $$\forall x\in \ZZ_+,\qquad q(x)\not=0,$$ and $$\forall x\in \ZZ_+,\qquad f(x)=\dfrac{p(x)}{q(x)}.$$
nodes.section: Polynomials and rational functions on the set of integers
differentia: there exist polynomials $p,q:\ZZ_+\longrightarrow\CC$ such that $$\forall x\in \ZZ_+,\qquad q(x)\not=0,$$ and $$\forall x\in \ZZ_+,\qquad f(x)=\dfrac{p(x)}{q(x)}.$$

nodes.name: Realization characterisation of rational functions
nodes.statement: Let $f:\ZZ_+\longrightarrow \CC$ be given. Then $f(x)$ is a rational function if and only if there exist a polynomial $p(x)$ and matrices $A,B,C$ such that \[ \sigma(A)\cap\ZZ_+=\emptyset, \] and \begin{equation} f(x)=p(x)+C(xI-A)^{-1}B. \end{equation}
nodes.section: Polynomials and rational functions on the set of integers
nodes.statement_short: $f$ is rational exactly when it has a state-space realization $p(x)+C(xI-A)^{-1}B$ with $\sigma(A)$ missing $\ZZ_+$.
conclusions: Then $f(x)$ is a rational function if and only if there exist a polynomial $p(x)$ and matrices $A,B,C$ such that \[ \sigma(A)\cap\ZZ_+=\emptyset, \] and \begin{equation} f(x)=p(x)+C(xI-A)^{-1}B. \end{equation}

nodes.name: Proof of the realization characterisation
nodes.statement: We first recall that a matrix-valued rational function of a complex variable can always be written in the form \[ r(z)=p(z)+C(zI-A)^{-1}B, \] where the matrix-valued polynomial $p$ takes care of the pole at infinity, and $A,B$ and $C$ are matrices of appropriate sizes. Furthermore, when the dimension of $A$ is minimal, the (finite) poles of $r$ coincide with the spectrum of $A$; see \cite{bgk1, MR0255260}. Here, we consider complex-valued functions, and thus $C$ and $B$ are respectively a row and column vector.\\ Now, by Definition \ref{defrat1}, $f$ is a rational function if and only if it is the restriction on $\ZZ_+$ of a rational function of a complex variable, with no poles on $\ZZ_+$, that is if and only if it can be written as \eqref{eqreal} with the matrix $A$ satisfying furthermore \eqref{kaas}.
nodes.section: Polynomials and rational functions on the set of integers
nodes.statement_short: Recall the classical minimal realization of a rational function of a complex variable, then restrict to $\ZZ_+$.

nodes.name: Growth bound for Fourier coefficients of rational functions
nodes.statement: Let $f:\ZZ_+\longrightarrow \CC$ be rational, and let $\hat {f}:\ZZ_+\longrightarrow \CC$ be the Fourier transform of $f$. Then $$\limsup_{n\rightarrow\infty}(|\hat f(n)|n!)^{1/n}\leq 1.$$
nodes.section: Polynomials and rational functions on the set of integers
nodes.statement_short: The Fourier coefficients of a rational $f$ satisfy $\limsup(|\hat f(n)|n!)^{1/n}\le 1$.
assumptions: Let $f:\ZZ_+\longrightarrow \CC$ be rational, and let $\hat {f}:\ZZ_+\longrightarrow \CC$ be the Fourier transform of $f$
conclusions: Then $$\limsup_{n\rightarrow\infty}(|\hat f(n)|n!)^{1/n}\leq 1.$$

nodes.name: Proof of the growth bound
nodes.statement: According to Proposition \ref{ABC}, there exist a polynomial $p(x)$ and matrices $A,B,C$ such that $\sigma(A)\cap\ZZ_+=\emptyset$ and $$f(x)=p(x)+C(xI-A)^{-1}B.$$ Hence, for $n>\deg(p)$, $$|\hat{f}(n)n!|=|(\delta^nf)(0)|\leq\|C\|\cdot\|B\|\cdot\|A^{-1}\|\cdot \prod_{j=1}^n\|\left(I-\dfrac{1}{n}A\right)^{-1}\|.$$ Since $$\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\|\left(I-\dfrac{1}{n}A\right)^{-1}\|=1,$$ $$\forall\epsilon>0,\,\,\exists M,N\in\ZZ_+,\,\forall n\in\ZZ_+\quad:\quad n\geq N\Longrightarrow|\hat{f}(n)n!|\leq M(1+\epsilon)^n,$$ and the conclusion follows.
nodes.section: Polynomials and rational functions on the set of integers
nodes.statement_short: Bound $|\hat f(n)n!|$ through the realization and use $\|(I-A/n)^{-1}\|\to1$.

nodes.name: Difference operators $\delta_x,\delta_y$
nodes.statement: The linear {\em difference operators} $\delta_x,\delta_y$ on the space of functions $f:\Omega_1\times\Omega_2\longrightarrow\CC$ are defined by $$(\delta_xf)(x,y):=f(x+1,y)-f(x,y),\quad (\delta_yf)(x,y):=f(x,y+1)-f(x,y).$$

nodes.name: Commutation of $\delta_x$ and $\delta_y$
nodes.statement: Note that the difference operators $\delta_x$ and $\delta_y$ commute: \[(\delta_x\delta_yf)(x,y)= (\delta_y\delta_xf)(x,y)=f(x+1,y+1)-f(x,y+1)-f(x+1,y)+f(x,y). \]
nodes.statement_short: The two partial difference operators commute, with the mixed difference given explicitly.

nodes.name: Finiteness of the two-variable transform
nodes.statement: Let $f:\ZZ_+^2\longrightarrow \CC$. Then for every $(x,y)\in\ZZ_+^2$, the series \[ \check f(x,y):=\sum_{(m,n)\in\ZZ_+^2}f(m,n)x^{[m]}y^{[n]} \] contains finitely many non-zero terms.
nodes.statement_short: The two-variable expansion $\check f(x,y)$ has finitely many nonzero terms.
conclusions: Then for every $(x,y)\in\ZZ_+^2$, the series \[ \check f(x,y):=\sum_{(m,n)\in\ZZ_+^2}f(m,n)x^{[m]}y^{[n]} \] contains finitely many non-zero terms.

nodes.name: Proof of two-variable finiteness
nodes.statement: In view of \eqref{poly}, $$\forall x\in\ZZ_+,\,\forall n\in\ZZ_+,\,\quad x<n\Longrightarrow x^{[n]}=0.$$ Therefore, for every $(x,y)\in\ZZ_+^2$ the series $\check f(x)$ contains at most $(x+1)(y+1)$ non-zero terms.
nodes.statement_short: As in one variable, $x^{[n]}=0$ for $n>x$, leaving at most $(x+1)(y+1)$ terms.

nodes.name: Two-variable inverse transform
nodes.statement: Let $f:\ZZ_+^2\longrightarrow \CC$. Then there exists a unique function $\hat f:\ZZ_+^2\longrightarrow \CC$ such that \[\forall (x,y)\in\ZZ_+^2, \qquad f(x,y)=\sum_{(m,n)\in\ZZ_+^2} \hat f(m,n)x^{[m]}y^{[n]}. \] The function $\hat f(m,n)$ is given by \[ \hat f(m,n)=\dfrac{(\delta_x^m\delta_y^nf)(0,0)}{m!n!}, \quad (m,n)\in\ZZ_+^2.\]
nodes.statement_short: Every $f$ on $\ZZ_+^2$ has a unique double $x^{[m]}y^{[n]}$ expansion with coefficients $(\delta_x^m\delta_y^nf)(0,0)/m!n!$.
conclusions: Then there exists a unique function $\hat f:\ZZ_+^2\longrightarrow \CC$ such that \[\forall (x,y)\in\ZZ_+^2, \qquad f(x,y)=\sum_{(m,n)\in\ZZ_+^2} \hat f(m,n)x^{[m]}y^{[n]}. \]
The function $\hat f(m,n)$ is given by \[ \hat f(m,n)=\dfrac{(\delta_x^m\delta_y^nf)(0,0)}{m!n!}, \quad (m,n)\in\ZZ_+^2.\]

nodes.name: Proof of the two-variable inverse transform
nodes.statement: First, fix $x\in\ZZ_+$ and consider the function $f_x:\ZZ_+\longrightarrow\CC$ given by $$f_x(y)=f(x,y),\quad y\in\ZZ_+.$$ Then, according to Proposition \ref{tay2}, there is a unique function $\hat{ f_x}:\ZZ_+\longrightarrow\CC$ such that $$\forall y\in\ZZ_+,\qquad f_x(y)=\sum_{n\in\ZZ_+}\hat{f_x}(n) y^{[n]};$$ the function $\hat{f_x}(n)$ is given by $$\hat{f_x}(n)=\dfrac{(\delta_y^n f)(x,0)}{n!},\quad n\in\ZZ_+.$$ Next, fix $n\in\ZZ_+$ and consider the function $g_n:\ZZ_+\longrightarrow \CC$ given by $$g_n(x)=\hat{f_x}(n),\quad x\in\ZZ_+.$$ By the same Proposition \ref{tay2}, there is a unique function $\hat{g_n}:\ZZ_+\longrightarrow \CC$ such that $$\forall x\in\ZZ_+,\qquad g_n(x)=\sum_{m\in\ZZ_+}\hat{g_n}(m) x^{[m]};$$ the function $\hat{g_n}(m)$ is given by $$\hat{g_n}(m)=\dfrac{(\delta_x^m\delta_y^n f)(0,0)}{m!n!},\quad m\in\ZZ_+.$$ Thus $$\forall (x,y)\in\ZZ_+^2,\qquad f(x,y)=\sum_{(m,n) \in\ZZ_+^2}\hat{g_n}(m) x^{[m]}y^{[n]}.$$ It remains to set $\hat f(m,n)=\hat{g_n}(m).$
nodes.statement_short: Apply the one-variable result in $y$ for fixed $x$, then again in $x$ to the resulting coefficients.

nodes.name: Fourier transform of $f:\ZZ_+^2\to\CC$
nodes.statement: Let $f:\ZZ_+^2\longrightarrow \CC$. Then the function $\hat f:\ZZ_+^2\longrightarrow\CC,$ defined by \eqref{fou11}, is said to be the Fourier transform of $f$.

nodes.name: A two-variable polynomial vanishing on $\ZZ^2$ is zero
nodes.statement: Let $p(z,w)$ be a complex polynomial in two variables. Then, $p\big|_{\ZZ^2}=0$ if and only if $p\equiv 0$.
assumptions: Let $p(z,w)$ be a complex polynomial in two variables
conclusions: Then, $p\big|_{\ZZ^2}=0$ if and only if $p\equiv 0$.

nodes.name: Proof that vanishing on $\ZZ^2$ forces $p\equiv0$
nodes.statement: Write \[ p(z,w)=\sum_{n=0}^N p_n(z)w^n, \] where the $p_n$ are polynomials in $z$. The equations $p(z,w)\equiv 0$ for $w=0,1,\ldots N$ lead to (using a Vandermonde determinant) that $p_0(z),p_1(z),\ldots, p_N(z)$ vanish on $\ZZ$ and hence identically.
nodes.statement_short: Expand in powers of $w$ and use a Vandermonde determinant to kill each coefficient polynomial.

nodes.name: Polynomial function on $\ZZ^2$
nodes.statement: Suppose that a function $f:\ZZ^2\longrightarrow\CC$ is such that $$\forall (x,y)\in\ZZ^2,\qquad f(x,y)=p(x,y),$$ where $p(x,y)$ is a polynomial with complex coefficients. Then in view of Theorem \ref{tautology}, such a polynomial $p(x,y)$ is unique, and we shall call the function $f$ itself a polynomial. If $f(x,y)\not\equiv 0,$ the degree of $f(x,y)$ is the same as the degree of $p(x,y)$.
nodes.statement_short: A function on $\ZZ^2$ agreeing with a (unique) two-variable complex polynomial is itself called a polynomial.
differentia: $$\forall (x,y)\in\ZZ^2,\qquad f(x,y)=p(x,y),$$ where $p(x,y)$ is a polynomial with complex coefficients

nodes.name: Finite support of $\hat f$ for polynomials on $\ZZ^2$
nodes.statement: Let $f:\ZZ^2\longrightarrow\CC$ be a polynomial, and let $\hat f :\ZZ_+^2\longrightarrow\CC$ be the Fourier transform of the restriction $f_{|_{\ZZ_+^2}}$. Then the function $\hat f$ has a finite support and $$\forall (x,y)\in\ZZ^2,\quad f(x,y)=\sum_{(m,n)\in\ZZ_+^2}\hat f(m,n)x^{[m]}y^{[n]}.$$
nodes.statement_short: A polynomial on $\ZZ^2$ has finitely supported transform and equals its double expansion everywhere.
assumptions: Let $f:\ZZ^2\longrightarrow\CC$ be a polynomial, and let $\hat f :\ZZ_+^2\longrightarrow\CC$ be the Fourier transform of the restriction $f_{|_{\ZZ_+^2}}$
conclusions: Then the function $\hat f$ has a finite support and $$\forall (x,y)\in\ZZ^2,\quad f(x,y)=\sum_{(m,n)\in\ZZ_+^2}\hat f(m,n)x^{[m]}y^{[n]}.$$

nodes.name: Proof of finite support on $\ZZ^2$
nodes.statement: First, in view of \eqref{fou11} and of the fact that $$\forall (m,n)\in\ZZ_+^2,\,\,\forall (x,y)\in\ZZ^2, \quad m+n>\deg(f)\Longrightarrow (\delta_x^m\delta_y^n f)(x,y)=0,$$ the function $\hat f$ has a finite support. It follows that $$\sum_{(m,n)\in\ZZ_+^2}\hat f(m,n)x^{[m]}y^{[n]}$$ is, in fact, a polynomial, which coincides with the polynomial $f(x,y)$ on $\ZZ_+^2$ and hence on $\ZZ^2$.
nodes.statement_short: High-order mixed differences of a polynomial vanish, so the expansion is a polynomial agreeing with $f$.

nodes.name: Polynomiality is preserved by $\delta_x,\delta_y$
nodes.statement: It follows from Proposition \ref{p11} and identity \eqref{hu2} that if $f:\ZZ^2\longrightarrow\CC$ is a polynomial then so are $\delta_x f$ and $\delta_yf$. A converse statement can be formulated as follows. It will be used in the proof of Theorem \ref{t1},
nodes.statement_short: Differences of polynomials are polynomials; the converse is the next proposition, needed for Theorem t1.

nodes.name: Two-variable discrete antiderivative under a compatibility condition
nodes.statement: Let $f,g:\ZZ^2\longrightarrow\CC$ be two polynomials, such that \[(\delta_y f)(x,y)\equiv(\delta_x g)(x,y).\] Then there exists a polynomial $h:\ZZ^2\longrightarrow\CC$ such that \[(\delta_xh)(x,y)\equiv f(x,y),\quad (\delta_yh)(x,y)\equiv g(x,y).\]
nodes.statement_short: If $\delta_y f\equiv\delta_x g$ then $f,g$ are the two partial differences of a single polynomial $h$.
assumptions: Let $f,g:\ZZ^2\longrightarrow\CC$ be two polynomials, such that \[(\delta_y f)(x,y)\equiv(\delta_x g)(x,y).\]
conclusions: Then there exists a polynomial $h:\ZZ^2\longrightarrow\CC$ such that \[(\delta_xh)(x,y)\equiv f(x,y),\quad (\delta_yh)(x,y)\equiv g(x,y).\]

nodes.name: Proof of the two-variable antiderivative
nodes.statement: By Proposition \ref{p11}, there exist functions $\hat f,\hat g:\ZZ_+^2\longrightarrow\CC$ with finite support, such that $$f(x,y)=\sum_{(m,n)\in\ZZ_+^2}\hat{f}(m,n)x^{[m]}y^{[n]},\quad g(x,y)=\sum_{(m,n)\in\ZZ_+^2}\hat{g}(m,n)x^{[m]}y^{[n]}.$$ Then identity \eqref{co01} implies that \[\forall (m,n)\in\ZZ^2_+,\qquad (n+1)\hat{f}(m,n+1)=(m+1)\hat{g}(m+1,n).\] Consider the polynomial $$h(x,y)=\sum_{(m,n)\in\ZZ_+^2}\dfrac{\hat{f}(m,n)}{m+1} x^{[m+1]}y^{[n]}+\sum_{n\in\ZZ_+}\dfrac{\hat{g}(0,n)}{n+1}y^{[n+1]},$$ then $$\forall (x,y)\in\ZZ^2,\qquad(\delta_x h)(x,y)=\sum_{(m,n)\in\ZZ_+^2}\hat{f}(m,n) x^{[m]}y^{[n]}=f(x,y).$$ On the other hand, in view of \eqref{use03}, $$h(x,y)=\sum_{(m,n)\in\ZZ_+^2}\dfrac{\hat{g}(m,n)}{n+1} x^{[m]}y^{[n+1]}+\sum_{n\in\ZZ_+}\dfrac{\hat{f}(m,0)}{m+1}x^{[m+1]},$$ hence $$\forall (x,y)\in\ZZ^2,\qquad(\delta_y h)(x,y)=\sum_{(m,n)\in\ZZ_+^2}\hat{g}(m,n) x^{[m]}y^{[n]}=g(x,y).$$
nodes.statement_short: Build $h$ from the coefficients of $f$, then verify $\delta_y h=g$ using the compatibility relation.

nodes.name: Discrete Cauchy-Riemann operator $\bar\cD$
nodes.statement: A function $f:\Omega_1\times\Omega_2\longrightarrow\CC$ is discrete analytic if and only if $$\forall (x,y)\in \Omega_1\times\Omega_2,\qquad(\bar\cD f)(x,y)=0,$$ where \[\bar\cD:=(1-i)\delta_x+(1+i)\delta_y+\delta_x\delta_y.\]
nodes.statement_short: Discrete analyticity is exactly membership in the kernel of $\bar\cD=(1-i)\delta_x+(1+i)\delta_y+\delta_x\delta_y$.
conclusions: is discrete analytic if and only if $$\forall (x,y)\in \Omega_1\times\Omega_2,\qquad(\bar\cD f)(x,y)=0,$$

nodes.name: Proof of the $\bar\cD$ characterisation
nodes.statement: In view of \eqref{comm}, \begin{multline*}\forall(x,y)\in\Omega_1\times\Omega_2,\quad \dfrac{f(x+1,y+1)-f(x,y)}{1+i}-\dfrac{f(x+1,y)-f(x,y+1)}{1-i}\\= \dfrac{1-i}{2}(f(x+1,y+1)-f(x,y)-if(x+1,y)+if(x,y+1))\\= \dfrac{1-i}{2}((\delta_x\delta_yf)(x,y)-2f(x,y)+ (1-i)f(x+1,y)+(1+i)f(x,y+1))\\=\dfrac{1-i}{2}((\delta_x\delta_yf)(x,y)+ (1-i)(\delta_xf)(x,y)+(1+i)(\delta_yf)(x,y)).\end{multline*}
nodes.statement_short: Direct algebraic rearrangement of the defining difference quotients using the commutation identity.

nodes.name: Non-uniqueness of discrete analytic extensions
nodes.statement: {\bf Extension:} In view of Definition \ref{maindef}, given $f_0\,\,:\,\,\ZZ\,\,\longrightarrow\,\,\mathbb C$ there are infinitely discrete analytic functions $f$ on $\ZZ^2$ such that $f(x,0)=f_0(x)$. However, the following theorem show that in the case when $f_0$ is a polynomial, only one of these discrete analytic extensions will be a polynomial in $x,y$. The result itself originates with the work of Duffin \cite{MR0078441}, and we give a new proof.
nodes.statement_short: Extensions from $\ZZ$ to $\ZZ^2$ are far from unique in general, but exactly one is polynomial.

nodes.name: Unique discrete analytic polynomial extension
nodes.statement: Let $p:\ZZ\longrightarrow\CC$ be a polynomial. Then there exists a unique discrete analytic polynomial $q:\ZZ^2\longrightarrow\CC$ such that $$\forall x\in\ZZ,\qquad q(x,0)= p(x).$$ In particular, $q(x,y)\equiv 0$ if and only if $p(x)\equiv 0$. If this is not the case, $$\deg(q)=\deg(p).$$
nodes.statement_short: Every polynomial on $\ZZ$ extends to a unique discrete analytic polynomial on $\ZZ^2$ of the same degree.
conclusions: Then there exists a unique discrete analytic polynomial $q:\ZZ^2\longrightarrow\CC$ such that $$\forall x\in\ZZ,\qquad q(x,0)= p(x).$$
In particular, $q(x,y)\equiv 0$ if and only if $p(x)\equiv 0$.
If this is not the case, $$\deg(q)=\deg(p).$$

nodes.name: A discrete analytic polynomial vanishing on the axis is zero
nodes.statement: Let $q:\ZZ^2\longrightarrow\CC$ be a discrete analytic polynomial, such that $q(x,0)\equiv 0.$ Then $q(x,y)\equiv 0.$
assumptions: Let $q:\ZZ^2\longrightarrow\CC$ be a discrete analytic polynomial, such that $q(x,0)\equiv 0.$
conclusions: Then $q(x,y)\equiv 0.$

nodes.name: Proof of the vanishing lemma
nodes.statement: Assume the opposite, then $\deg(q)>0,$ and $q$ can be chosen so that $\deg q$ is the smallest possible. Observe that $(\delta_xq)(x,y)$ is also a discrete analytic polynomial, that $ (\delta_xq)(x,0)\equiv 0,$ and that $\deg(\delta_xp)<\deg(p).$ Hence $(\delta_xq)(x,y)\equiv 0.$ Since $q(x,y)$ is discrete analytic, Definition \ref{maindef2} implies that $$\forall (x,y)\in\ZZ^2,\qquad (\delta_yq)(x,y)= \dfrac{i-1}{2}((1-i+\delta_y)\delta_xq)(x,y)= 0.$$ Thus $$(\delta_xq)(x,y)\equiv(\delta_yq)(x,y)\equiv 0$$ and hence $q=\const$ - a contradiction.
nodes.statement_short: Minimal-degree counterexample: $\delta_x q$ vanishes, hence so does $\delta_y q$, forcing $q$ constant.

nodes.name: Proof of the unique discrete analytic polynomial extension
nodes.statement: The uniqueness of the polynomial $q(x,y)$ follows from Lemma \ref{l1}. The existence in the case $p=\const$ is clear: it suffices to set $$q(x,y)=p(0).$$ If $p\not=\const$ we proceed by induction on $d=\deg(p)$. According to Proposition \ref{p03}, $(\delta p)(x)$ is a polynomial and $\deg(\delta p)=d-1$. Therefore, by the induction assumption, there is a discrete analytic polynomial $f(x,y)$, such that $$\forall x\in\ZZ,\qquad f(x,0)=(\delta p)(x)$$ and $\deg(f)=d-1.$ Let $g:\ZZ^2\longrightarrow\CC$ be defined by $$g(x,y)=if(x,y)-\dfrac{1-i}{2}(\delta_yf)(x,y),$$ then $g(x,y)$ is also a discrete analytic polynomial, $\deg(g)=d-1.$ Furthermore, since $(\bar Df)(x,y)\equiv 0,$ \begin{multline*}\forall (x,y)\in\ZZ^2,\quad (\delta_xg)(x,y)=i(\delta_xf)(x,y)-\dfrac{1-i}{2}(\delta_x\delta_yf)(x,y)\\= i(\delta_xf)(x,y)+\dfrac{1-i}{2}((1-i)(\delta_xf)(x,y)+(1+i)(\delta_yf)(x,y))= (\delta_yf)(x,y).\end{multline*} Hence, according to Proposition \ref{p13}, there exists a polynomial $h:\ZZ^2\longrightarrow\CC$ such that $$(\delta_xh)(x,y)\equiv f(x,y),\quad (\delta_y h)(x,y)\equiv g(x,y).$$ Since $$\forall (x,y)\in\ZZ^2,\qquad (\bar D h)(x,y)=(1-i)f(x,y)+(1+i)g(x,y)+(\delta_y f)(x,y)=0,$$ the polynomial $h(x,y)$ is discrete analytic. Finally, since $$\forall x\in\ZZ,\qquad (\delta_x h)(x,0)=f(x,0)=(\delta p)(x),$$ $h(x,0)-p(x)$ is a constant function. Thus it suffices to set $$q(x,y)=h(x,y)-h(0,0)+p(0)$$ to complete the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Uniqueness from the lemma; existence by induction on $\deg p$, building $h$ via the two-variable antiderivative.

nodes.name: Discrete analytic polynomials $\zeta_n$
nodes.statement: In view of Theorem \ref{t1}, there exists a unique discrete analytic polynomial $\zeta_n(x,y)$ determined by $$\zeta_n(x,0)\equiv x^{[n]}.$$
nodes.statement_short: $\zeta_n$ is the unique discrete analytic polynomial restricting to $x^{[n]}$ on the horizontal axis.

nodes.name: Difference relation $(\delta_x\zeta_n)\equiv n\zeta_{n-1}$
nodes.statement: Hence, by the uniqueness part of Theorem \ref{t1}, \[(\delta_x\zeta_n)(x,y)\equiv n\zeta_{n-1}(x,y)\] (if $n=0$, $\zeta_0(x,y)\equiv 1$ and $(\delta_x\zeta_0)(x,y)\equiv 0$).
nodes.statement_short: The $\zeta_n$ obey the same lowering rule under $\delta_x$ as the $x^{[n]}$ under $\delta$.

nodes.name: Generating function $e_{x,y}(z)$ of the $\zeta_n$
nodes.statement: For each $(x,y)\in\ZZ^2$ the function \[ e_{x,y}(z)=(1+z)^x\left(\dfrac{1+i+iz}{1+i+z}\right)^y, \] is analytic (in the usual sense) in the variable $z$ in the open unit disk $\mathbb D$, and admits the Taylor expansion \begin{equation} e_{x,y}(z)=\sum_{n\in\ZZ_+}\dfrac{z^n \zeta_n(x,y)}{n!},\quad \forall z\in\DD. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: $e_{x,y}(z)=(1+z)^x((1+i+iz)/(1+i+z))^y$ is analytic on $\DD$ and generates the $\zeta_n(x,y)/n!$.
conclusions: is analytic (in the usual sense) in the variable $z$ in the open unit disk $\mathbb D$
and admits the Taylor expansion \begin{equation} e_{x,y}(z)=\sum_{n\in\ZZ_+}\dfrac{z^n \zeta_n(x,y)}{n!},\quad \forall z\in\DD. \end{equation}

nodes.name: Proof of the generating-function expansion
nodes.statement: The analyticity is clear because $x,y\in\ZZ$ and we have $$e_{x,y}(z)=\sum_{n\in\ZZ_+}\dfrac{z^n c_n(x,y)}{n!},\quad \forall z\in\DD.$$ where $$c_n(x,y)=\dfrac{d^n}{dz^n}e_{x,y}\Bigm|_{z=0}.$$ Since $$e_{x+1,y}(z)-e_{x,y}(z)=ze_{x,y}(z)=\sum_{n\in\ZZ_+}\dfrac{z^{n+1} c_{n}(x,y)}{n!},$$ $$\forall (x,y)\in\ZZ^2,\,\,\forall n\in\ZZ_+,\qquad (\delta_xc_{n})(x,y)=nc_{n-1}(x,y)$$ (if $n=0,$ $c_0(x,y)\equiv 1$ and $(\delta_xc_0)(x,y)\equiv 0$). Similarly, since \[ \begin{split} \dfrac{e_{x+1,y+1}(z)-e_{x,y}(z)}{1+ i}-\dfrac{e_{x+1,y}(z)-e_{x,y+1}(z)}{1-i}&=\\ &\hspace{-5cm}=\left( (1+z)\dfrac{1+i+iz}{1+i+z}-1\right)\dfrac{e_{x,y}(z)}{1+i}-\left( 1+z-\dfrac{1+i+iz}{1+i+z}\right)\dfrac{e_{x,y}(z)}{1-i}\\ &\hspace{-5cm}=0, \end{split} \] we have $$\forall (x,y)\in\ZZ^2,\,\,{\rm and}\,\,\forall n\in\ZZ_+,\qquad (\bar Dc_{n})(x,y)=0.$$ Thus, for every $n\in\ZZ_+$, the function $c_n:\ZZ^2\longrightarrow\CC$ is discrete analytic. Next, we show by induction that \[ \forall n\in\ZZ_+,\quad c_n(x,y)\equiv\zeta_n(x,y). \] Indeed, for $n=0$, $$c_0(x,y)\equiv 1\equiv\zeta_0(x,y).$$ Assume that, for some $n\in\ZZ_+$, $$c_n(x,y)\equiv\zeta_n(x,y),$$ then, in view of \eqref{hu3}, $$(\delta_xc_{n+1}(x,y)\equiv(n+1)c_n(x,y)\equiv (n+1)\zeta_n(x,y)\equiv(\delta_x\zeta_{n+1}(x,y),$$ hence $$(\delta_x(\zeta_{n+1}-c_{n+1}))(x,y)\equiv 0.$$ But the functions $c_{n+1}$ and $\zeta_{n+1}$ are discrete analytic, hence $$(\bar D(\zeta_{n+1}-c_{n+1}))(x,y)\equiv 0$$ and $$(\delta_y(\zeta_{n+1}-c_{n+1}))(x,y)\equiv 0.$$ It follows that $$\zeta_{n+1}-c_{n+1}=\const;$$ since $$\zeta_{n+1}(0,0)=0=c_{n+1}(0,0),$$ one concludes that $$c_{n+1}(x,y)\equiv\zeta_{n+1}(x,y),$$ and \eqref{hu4} follows.
nodes.statement_short: Show the Taylor coefficients $c_n$ are discrete analytic and satisfy the same recursion, then identify $c_n\equiv\zeta_n$ by induction.

nodes.name: Values of $\zeta_n(x,0)$
nodes.statement: Let $x,n\in\mathbb Z_+$. Then, \[ \zeta_n(x,0)=\begin{cases} x(x-1)\cdots (x-n+1)=x^{[n]},\,\, if\quad n\le x\\ \quad0,\quad \hspace{3.82cm}if \quad n>x. \end{cases} \]
conclusions: Then, \[ \zeta_n(x,0)=\begin{cases} x(x-1)\cdots (x-n+1)=x^{[n]},\,\, if\quad n\le x\\ \quad0,\quad \hspace{3.82cm}if \quad n>x. \end{cases} \]

nodes.name: Proof of the values of $\zeta_n(x,0)$
nodes.statement: Set $y=0$ in $e_{x,y}(z)$ in \eqref{exy}. By \eqref{hu4} we get \[ (1+z)^x=\sum_{n\in\ZZ_+}\frac{z^n}{n!}\zeta_n(x,0). \] \eqref{value:zeta:n} follows by comparing the coefficients of $z^n$ in \eqref{eq:y=0}.
nodes.statement_short: Set $y=0$ in the generating function and compare coefficients of $z^n$.

nodes.name: Growth rate of $\zeta_n$
nodes.statement: It holds that $$\forall(x,y)\in\ZZ_+\times (\ZZ\setminus\{0\}),\qquad \limsup_{n\rightarrow\infty} \left(\dfrac{|\zeta_n(x,y)|}{n!}\right)^{1/n}= \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}.$$
nodes.statement_short: Off the horizontal axis, $(|\zeta_n(x,y)|/n!)^{1/n}$ has $\limsup$ exactly $1/\sqrt{2}$.
conclusions: \limsup_{n\rightarrow\infty} \left(\dfrac{|\zeta_n(x,y)|}{n!}\right)^{1/n}= \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}.$$

nodes.name: Proof of the growth rate of $\zeta_n$
nodes.statement: When $x\ge 0$ the function \eqref{exy} is analytic in the variable $z$ in the disk centered at the origin and of radius $\sqrt{2}$, and has a pole on the boundary of this disk. Hence the radius of convergence of the McLaurin series is precisely $\sqrt{2}$, and $$\limsup_{n\rightarrow\infty} \left(\dfrac{|\zeta_n(x,y)|}{n!}\right)^{1/n}= \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}.$$
nodes.statement_short: The generating function has radius of convergence $\sqrt{2}$ with a pole on that circle.

nodes.name: Absolutely convergent $\zeta_n$-series are discrete analytic
nodes.statement: Let $g:\ZZ_+\longrightarrow\CC$ be such that for every $(x,y)\in\ZZ_+\times\ZZ$ the series \[f(x,y)=\sum_{n\in\ZZ_+} g(n)\zeta_n(x,y)\] converges absolutely. Then the function $f:\ZZ_+\times \ZZ\longrightarrow \CC$, defined by \eqref{tay41}, is discrete analytic, and it holds that $$g(n)\equiv \hat{f_0}(n),$$ where the function $f_0:\ZZ_+\longrightarrow\CC$ is given by \[f_0(x)=f(x,0),\quad x\in\ZZ_+.\]
nodes.statement_short: An absolutely convergent series $\sum g(n)\zeta_n$ is discrete analytic and $g$ is the Fourier transform of its restriction.
assumptions: Let $g:\ZZ_+\longrightarrow\CC$ be such that for every $(x,y)\in\ZZ_+\times\ZZ$ the series \[f(x,y)=\sum_{n\in\ZZ_+} g(n)\zeta_n(x,y)\] converges absolutely.
conclusions: Then the function $f:\ZZ_+\times \ZZ\longrightarrow \CC$, defined by \eqref{tay41}, is discrete analytic, and it holds that $$g(n)\equiv \hat{f_0}(n),$$

nodes.name: Proof that $\zeta_n$-series are discrete analytic
nodes.statement: The discrete analyticity of $f$ follows directly from the discrete analyticity of the polynomials $\zeta_n$. Furthermore, when $y=0$ the formula \eqref{tay41} becomes $$f_0(x)=\sum_{n\in\ZZ_+} g(n)x^{[n]},$$ hence, according to Proposition \ref{tay2}, $g=\hat{f_0}$.
nodes.statement_short: Discrete analyticity is inherited termwise; setting $y=0$ identifies $g$ with $\hat{f_0}$.

nodes.name: Expandable function
nodes.statement: A function $f:\ZZ_+\times \ZZ\longrightarrow \CC$ is said to be {\em expandable} if:\begin{enumerate} \item the Fourier transform $\hat{f_0}$ of the function $f_0:\ZZ_+\longrightarrow\CC$, given by \eqref{rest}, satisfies the estimate \begin{equation} \limsup_{n\rightarrow\infty}(|\hat{f_0}(n)|n!)^{1/n}<\sqrt{2}; \end{equation} \item the function $f$ admits the representation $$ f(x,y)=\sum_{n\in\ZZ_+}\hat{f_0}(n)\zeta_n(x,y),\quad (x,y)\in\ZZ_+\times\ZZ.$$ \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: An expandable function is one whose restriction has Fourier coefficients below the $\sqrt{2}$ growth threshold and which equals its $\zeta_n$-expansion.
differentia: \item the Fourier transform $\hat{f_0}$ of the function $f_0:\ZZ_+\longrightarrow\CC$, given by \eqref{rest}, satisfies the estimate \begin{equation} \limsup_{n\rightarrow\infty}(|\hat{f_0}(n)|n!)^{1/n}<\sqrt{2}; \end{equation}

nodes.name: Scope of the expandable class
nodes.statement: The class of expandable functions contains all discrete analytic polynomials, and elements of this class are determined by their values on the positive horizontal axis.
conclusions: The class of expandable functions contains all discrete analytic polynomials
elements of this class are determined by their values on the positive horizontal axis.

nodes.name: Unique expandable extension of a rational function
nodes.statement: Suppose that $f_0:\ZZ_+\longrightarrow \CC$ is rational. Then there exists a unique expandable function $f:\ZZ_+\times \ZZ\longrightarrow \CC$ such that $$f(x,0)\equiv f_0(x).$$
conclusions: Then there exists a unique expandable function $f:\ZZ_+\times \ZZ\longrightarrow \CC$ such that $$f(x,0)\equiv f_0(x).$$

nodes.name: Proof of the unique expandable extension
nodes.statement: This is a consequence of Theorem \ref{lim1}.
nodes.statement_short: Cites Theorem lim1.

nodes.name: Cauchy-Kovalevskaya product $\odot$
nodes.statement: Consider $f_1$ and $f_2$ two expandable functions, and assume that the Fourier transform of the pointwise product $f_1(x,0)f_2(x,0)$ satisfy \eqref{esti}. Then there exists a unique discrete analytic expandable function $g$ such that \[ g(x,0)=f_1(x,0)f_2(x,0) \] $g$ is called the Cauchy-Kovalesvskaya product of $f_1$ and $f_2$ and is denoted by $f_1\odot f_2$.
nodes.statement_short: The C-K product of two expandable functions is the unique expandable extension of the pointwise product of their restrictions.
nodes.genus: a unique discrete analytic expandable function $g$

nodes.name: C-K product of rational functions always exists
nodes.statement: Note that the Cauchy-Kovalesvskaya product of two rational functions always exist.
conclusions: the Cauchy-Kovalesvskaya product of two rational functions always exist.

nodes.name: Formal C-K product via $\cZ$
nodes.statement: Let $f:\ZZ^2\longrightarrow \CC$ be a polynomial, such that $$f(x,0)\equiv c_0+c_1x+\dots +c_nx^n,$$ and let $g:\Omega\times\ZZ\longrightarrow \CC$ be given. The Cauchy-Kovalevskaya (C-K) product of $f$ and $g$ is defined by \begin{equation} (g\odot f)(x,y)=(f\odot g)(x,y)=c_0g(x,y)+c_1(\cZ g)(x,y)+\dots+c_n(\cZ^ng)(x,y). \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Formally, $f\odot g=f(\cZ)g$: substitute the multiplication operator $\cZ$ into the coefficient polynomial of $f$.

nodes.name: Properties of the C-K product
nodes.statement: \mbox{}\\ $(1)$ The restriction of the C-K product to $\mathbb Z_+$ is the product of the restriction.\\ $(2)$ The C-K product is the unique discrete analytic extension corresponding to the product of the restrictions.\\ $(3)$ The C-K product is commutative, i.e. \[ g\odot f=f\odot g \] for all choices of discrete analytic polynomials
nodes.statement_short: The C-K product restricts to the pointwise product on $\ZZ_+$, is the unique discrete analytic extension of it, and is commutative.
assumptions: for all choices of discrete analytic polynomials
conclusions: $(1)$ The restriction of the C-K product to $\mathbb Z_+$ is the product of the restriction.
$(2)$ The C-K product is the unique discrete analytic extension corresponding to the product of the restrictions.
$(3)$ The C-K product is commutative, i.e. \[ g\odot f=f\odot g \]

nodes.name: Proof of the properties of the C-K product
nodes.statement: \mbox{}\\ $(1)$ Setting $y=0$ in \eqref{ckdef} and taking into account the definition of $\cZ$ we have \[ \begin{split} (g\odot f)(x,0)&=c_0g(x,0)+c_1(\cZ g)(x,0)+\dots+c_n(\cZ^ng)(x,0)\\ &=c_0g(x,0)+c_1xg(x,0)+\cdots +c_nx^ng(x,0)\\ &=f(x,0)g(x,0). \end{split} \] $(2)$ For an expandable function the discrete Cauchy-Riemann equation $\overline{D}f=0$ with prescribed initial values on the horizontal positive axis has a unique solution (see Theorem \ref{p52}).\\ $(3)$ is then clear from $(1)$ and $(2)$.
nodes.statement_short: Set $y=0$ to get (1), invoke uniqueness of discrete analytic extensions for (2), and deduce (3).

nodes.name: Origin of the name Cauchy-Kovalevskaya product
nodes.statement: We now explain the name given to this product. Recall that the classical Cauchy-Kovalevskaya theorem concerns uniqueness of solutions of certain partial differential equations with given initial conditions. See for instance \cite{MR93j:26013}. In Clifford analysis, where the pointwise product of hyperholomorphic functions need not be hyperholomorphic, this theorem was used by F. Sommen in \cite{MR618518} (see also \cite{bds}) to define the product of hyperholomorphic quaternionic-valued functions in $\mathbb R^4$ by extending the pointwise product from an hyperplane. In the present setting of expandable functions the discrete Cauchy-Riemann equation $\overline{D}f=0$ with prescribed initial values on the horizontal positive axis also has a unique solution. This is why the pointwise product on the horizontal positive axis can be extended to a unique expandable function, which we call the C-K product.
nodes.statement_short: The name mirrors Sommen's Clifford-analysis construction: extend a pointwise product off an initial hyperplane using uniqueness for the CR equation.

nodes.name: C-K product with a discrete analytic polynomial
nodes.statement: If $p$ is a discrete analytic polynomial and $f$ is an expandable function, $p\odot f$ is the expandable function determined by \[ (p\odot f)(x,0)=p(x,0)f(x,0). \]
assumptions: If $p$ is a discrete analytic polynomial and $f$ is an expandable function
conclusions: $p\odot f$ is the expandable function determined by \[ (p\odot f)(x,0)=p(x,0)f(x,0). \]

nodes.name: $e_{x,y}(t)$: pointwise square of an expandable restriction need not be expandable
nodes.statement: However it is not true in general that the pointwise product of the restrictions of two expandable functions, say $f$ and $g$, is itself the restriction of an expandable function, as is illustrated by the example \[ f(x,y)=g(x,y)=e_{x,y}(t), \] where $e_{x,y}(t)$ is defined by \eqref{exy} and $|t|>$. Indeed, \[ e_{x,0}(t)=(1+t)^x \] is the restriction of an expandable function whenever $|t|<\sqrt{2}$. On the other hand, $(e_{x,0}(t))^2=e_{x,0}(2t+t^2)$ will not be the restriction of an expandable function for $|t|>\sqrt{1+\sqrt{2}}-1$ which is strictly smaller than $\sqrt{2}$.
nodes.statement_short: Squaring $e_{x,0}(t)=(1+t)^x$ breaks the $\sqrt{2}$ growth threshold, so the pointwise product escapes the expandable class.

nodes.name: C-K product of two $\zeta$'s
nodes.statement: For $m,n\in\ZZ_+$ and $j\in\left\{0,\ldots, m+n\right\}$, set \[ c^{m,n}_j=\frac{\delta^j\left(x^{[m]}x^{[n]}\right)}{j!}|_{x=0}. \] Then, \[ \zeta_m\odot\zeta_n=\sum_{j=0}^{m+n}c_j^{m,n}\zeta_j. \]
nodes.statement_short: $\zeta_m\odot\zeta_n$ expands in the $\zeta_j$ with the connection coefficients of $x^{[m]}x^{[n]}$.
conclusions: Then, \[ \zeta_m\odot\zeta_n=\sum_{j=0}^{m+n}c_j^{m,n}\zeta_j. \]

nodes.name: Proof of the $\zeta_m\odot\zeta_n$ expansion
nodes.statement: It suffices to note that \eqref{equalzeta} holds for $y=0$, thanks to Proposition \ref{tay2}.
nodes.statement_short: Check the identity at $y=0$ and invoke uniqueness of the $x^{[n]}$-expansion.

nodes.name: Link to discrete hypergroups
nodes.statement: Systems like \eqref{equalzeta} occur in the theory of discrete hypergroups. See \cite{MR2606478}.
nodes.statement_short: Such linearization systems are the structure constants studied in discrete hypergroup theory.

nodes.name: Multiplication operator $\cZ$
nodes.statement: The {\em multiplication operator} $\cZ$ on the class of functions $f:\Omega\times\ZZ\longrightarrow \CC$ is given by $$(\cZ f)(x,y)=xf(x,y)+iy\dfrac{f(x,y+1)+f(x,y-1)}{2}.$$
nodes.statement_short: $\cZ$ is the discrete counterpart of multiplication by the complex variable, mixing $xf$ with a $y$-average of $f$.

nodes.name: Basic properties of $\cZ$
nodes.statement: Let $f$ be a function from $\Omega\times \ZZ$ into $\mathbb C$. Then\\ $(1)$ \[(\cZ f)(x,0)\equiv xf(x,0). \] Furthermore:\\ $(2)$ If $f$ is a polynomial, then so is $\cZ f.$\\ $(3)$ If $f$ is discrete analytic, then so is $\cZ f$.
nodes.statement_short: $\cZ$ restricts to multiplication by $x$ on the axis and preserves polynomials and discrete analyticity.
assumptions: Let $f$ be a function from $\Omega\times \ZZ$ into $\mathbb C$
conclusions: $(2)$ If $f$ is a polynomial, then so is $\cZ f.$
$(3)$ If $f$ is discrete analytic, then so is $\cZ f$.

nodes.name: Proof of the basic properties of $\cZ$
nodes.statement: The proofs of $(1)$ and $(2)$ are clear from the definition. The proof of $(3)$ follows from the identity \eqref{id3} in Theorem \ref{tm34}.
nodes.statement_short: Parts (1),(2) are immediate from the definition; (3) follows from the commutator identity with $\overline{D}$.

nodes.name: $\cZ$ preserves expandability
nodes.statement: Let $f:\ZZ_+\times\ZZ\longrightarrow \CC$ be expandable. Then so is $\cZ f$. In particular, \[ \forall n\in\ZZ_+,\qquad (\cZ\zeta_n)(x,y)\equiv \zeta_{n+1}(x,y)+n\zeta_n(x,y). \]
nodes.statement_short: $\cZ$ maps expandable functions to expandable functions, acting on the basis by $\cZ\zeta_n=\zeta_{n+1}+n\zeta_n$.
conclusions: Then so is $\cZ f$.
In particular, \[ \forall n\in\ZZ_+,\qquad (\cZ\zeta_n)(x,y)\equiv \zeta_{n+1}(x,y)+n\zeta_n(x,y). \]

nodes.name: Proof that $\cZ$ preserves expandability
nodes.statement: By Proposition \ref{ok}, for every $n\in\ZZ_+$, $(\cZ\zeta_n)(x,y)$ is a discrete analytic polynomial. In view of \eqref{xmult}, $$(\cZ\zeta_n)(x,0)= x\cdot x^{[n]}=x^{[n+1]}+n x^{[n]},$$ hence formula \eqref{hu5} follows from Theorem \ref{t1}. Let $f_0:\ZZ_+\longrightarrow\CC$ be defined by \eqref{rest}, then $$(\cZ f)(x,0)= xf_0(x)=\sum_{n\in\ZZ_+}(n\hat{f_0}(n)+\hat{f_0}(n-1))x^{[n]},$$ where $\hat{f_0}(-1):=0.$ Since $$\limsup_{n\rightarrow\infty}(|\hat{f_0}(n)|n!)^{1/n}<\sqrt{2},$$ $$\limsup_{n\rightarrow\infty}(|n\hat{f_0}(n)+\hat{f_0}(n-1)|n!)^{1/n}<\sqrt{2}.$$ Finally, since $$f(x,y)=\sum_{n\in\ZZ_+}\hat{f_0}(n)\zeta_n(x,y),$$ where the convergence is absolute, $$(\cZ f)(x,y)=\sum_{n\in\ZZ_+}\hat{f_0}(n)(\cZ \zeta_n)(x,y)=\sum_{n\in\ZZ_+}(n\hat{f_0}(n)+\hat{f_0}(n-1))\zeta_n(x,y).$$
nodes.statement_short: Compute $\cZ\zeta_n$ on the axis and lift by uniqueness, then check the growth estimate survives the recursion.

nodes.name: $\zeta_1\odot\zeta_n=\cZ\zeta_n$
nodes.statement: From the preceeding proof we note that \[ \zeta_1\odot \zeta_n=\cZ \zeta_n=n\zeta_n+\zeta_{n+1}. \]
nodes.statement_short: C-K multiplication by $\zeta_1$ coincides with the action of $\cZ$.

nodes.name: Lie algebra generated by $\delta_x,\delta_y,\cZ,\overline{D}$
nodes.statement: The operators $\delta_x,\delta_y, \mathcal Z$ and $\overline{D}$ generate a Lie algebra of linear operators on the space of all functions from $\ZZ^2$ into $\mathbb C$. The Lie bracket is $[A,B]=AB-BA$ and the relations on the generators are \newcommand{\de}{\delta} \begin{align} [\delta_x,\cZ]&=1+\delta_x,\\ [\de_y,\cZ]&= i(1+\de_y+\de_y^2),\\ [\overline{D},\cZ]&=\left(\frac{1+i}{2}+\frac{i}{2}\de_y\right)\overline{D},\\ [\overline{D},\de_x]&=[\overline{D},\de_y]=[\de_x,\de_y]=0. \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: The four operators close under commutators into a Lie algebra with the listed relations.
conclusions: The operators $\delta_x,\delta_y, \mathcal Z$ and $\overline{D}$ generate a Lie algebra of linear operators on the space of all functions from $\ZZ^2$ into $\mathbb C$.

\begin{align} [\delta_x,\cZ]&=1+\delta_x,\\ [\de_y,\cZ]&= i(1+\de_y+\de_y^2),\\ [\overline{D},\cZ]&=\left(\frac{1+i}{2}+\frac{i}{2}\de_y\right)\overline{D},\\ [\overline{D},\de_x]&=[\overline{D},\de_y]=[\de_x,\de_y]=0. \end{align}

nodes.name: Proof of the commutation relations
nodes.statement: The identities \eqref{id1}-\eqref{id2} can be verified by the calculations in the proofs of the two preceding propositions.
nodes.statement_short: The relations are read off from the computations in the two preceding propositions.

nodes.name: Rational discrete analytic function
nodes.statement: A function $f:\ZZ_+\times\ZZ\longrightarrow\CC$ is said to be a {\em rational discrete analytic} function if $f(x,y)$ is expandable and $f(x,0)$ is rational.

nodes.name: Rational $=$ C-K quotient of discrete analytic polynomials
nodes.statement: An expandable function $f:\ZZ_+\times\ZZ\longrightarrow\CC$ is rational if and only if it is a C-K quotient of discrete analytic polynomials function that is, if and only if there exist discrete analytic polynomials $p(x,y)$ and $q(x,y)$ such that $$\forall x\in\ZZ_+,\qquad q(x,0)\not=0$$ and $$(q\odot f)(x,y)\equiv p(x,y).$$
nodes.statement_short: An expandable $f$ is rational exactly when $q\odot f=p$ for discrete analytic polynomials $p,q$ with $q(\cdot,0)$ nonvanishing.
conclusions: is rational if and only if it is a C-K quotient of discrete analytic polynomials function that is, if and only if there exist discrete analytic polynomials $p(x,y)$ and $q(x,y)$ such that $$\forall x\in\ZZ_+,\qquad q(x,0)\not=0$$ and $$(q\odot f)(x,y)\equiv p(x,y).$$

nodes.name: Proof of the C-K quotient characterisation
nodes.statement: Suppose first that $f$ is rational, and let $f_0(x)$ denote the restriction of $f$ to the horizontal positive axis. By definition there exists two polynomials $p_0(x)$ and $q_0(x)$ such that $q_0(x)\not=0$ (on $\ZZ_+$) and \[ q_0(x)f_0(x)=p_0(x),\quad x\in\ZZ_+. \] Let $p(x,y)$ and $q(x,y)$ denote the discrete analytic polynomials extending $p_0(x)$ and $q_0(x)$ respectively. Then both $p$ and $q\odot f$ are expandable functions, which coincide on $\ZZ_+$, and therefore everywhere.\\ Conversely, let $p(x,y)$ and $q(x,y)$ be the discrete analytic polynomials such that $$\forall x\in\ZZ_+,\qquad q(x,0)\not=0$$and $$(q\odot f)(x,y)\equiv p(x,y).$$ Setting $y=0$ leads to $$\forall x\in\ZZ_+,\quad q(x,0)f(x,0)=p(x,0),$$ which ends the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Both directions by extending/restricting to the horizontal axis, where the C-K product is pointwise.

nodes.name: Existence and uniqueness of the C-K quotient
nodes.statement: Let $p(x,y)$ and $q(x,y)$ be the discrete analytic polynomials such that $$\forall x\in\ZZ_+,\qquad q(x,0)\not=0$$ Then there is a unique expandable rational function $f$ such that $$(q\odot f)(x,y)\equiv p(x,y).$$
nodes.statement_short: For discrete analytic polynomials $p,q$ with $q(\cdot,0)\ne0$ there is exactly one expandable rational $f$ with $q\odot f=p$.
assumptions: Let $p(x,y)$ and $q(x,y)$ be the discrete analytic polynomials such that $$\forall x\in\ZZ_+,\qquad q(x,0)\not=0$$
conclusions: Then there is a unique expandable rational function $f$ such that $$(q\odot f)(x,y)\equiv p(x,y).$$

nodes.name: Proof of existence and uniqueness of the C-K quotient
nodes.statement: Denote $$g(x,y)=(q\odot f)(x,y).$$ According to Proposition \ref{ok2}, the function $g:\ZZ_+\times\ZZ\longrightarrow\CC$ is expandable, and therefore can be written as $$g(x,y)=\sum_{n\in\ZZ_+}\hat{g_0}(n)\zeta_n(x,y),$$ where $\hat{g_0}$ is the Fourier transform of its restriction $$g_0(x)=g(x,0).$$ In particular, by Theorem \ref{p52}, $g$ is discrete analytic. In view of \eqref{xmult}, $$g_0(x)=q(x,0)f(x,0)=p(x,0),$$ hence, by Proposition \ref{p01}, $\hat{g_0}$ has finite support and $g$ is a discrete analytic polynomial. In view of Theorem \ref{t1}, $$g(x,y)\equiv p(x,y).$$
nodes.statement_short: $q\odot f$ is expandable with finitely supported transform, hence a discrete analytic polynomial equal to $p$.

nodes.name: The reproducing kernel Hilbert space $\cH_{DA}$
nodes.statement: We denote by $\cH_{DA}$ the reproducing kernel Hilbert space with reproducing kernel \[ K((x_1,y_1),(x_2,y_2))= \sum_{n=0}^\infty\dfrac{\zeta_n(x_1,y_1)\zeta_n(x_2,y_2)^*}{(n!)^2}, \] and let $e_n:=\frac{1}{n!}\zeta_n$ be the corresponding ONB in $\cH_{DA}$.
nodes.section: The $C^*$-algebra associated to expandable discrete analytic functions
nodes.statement_short: $\cH_{DA}$ is the RKHS whose kernel sums $\zeta_n(x_1,y_1)\overline{\zeta_n(x_2,y_2)}/(n!)^2$, with ONB $e_n=\zeta_n/n!$.

nodes.name: $\delta_x$ is a copy of the backwards shift
nodes.statement: \begin{equation} \delta_xe_1=0\quad{and}\quad \delta_xe_n=e_{n-1},\quad n>1, \end{equation} i.e., $\delta_x$ is a copy of the backwards shift.
nodes.section: The $C^*$-algebra associated to expandable discrete analytic functions
assumptions: let $e_n:=\frac{1}{n!}\zeta_n$ be the corresponding ONB in $\cH_{DA}$
conclusions: \begin{equation} \delta_xe_1=0\quad{and}\quad \delta_xe_n=e_{n-1},\quad n>1, \end{equation} i.e., $\delta_x$ is a copy of the backwards shift.

nodes.name: Proof that $\delta_x$ is the backwards shift
nodes.statement: Using Proposition \ref{prop6.1}, we get \begin{equation} \delta_xe_{x,y}(z)=e_{x+1,y}(z)-e_{x,y}(z)=ze_{x,y}(z). \end{equation} Substituting the expression $e_{x,y}(z)=\sum_{n\in\ZZ_+}\frac{z^n}{n!}\zeta_n(x,y)$ into \eqref{eq1234}, we get $\delta_x\zeta_1=0$ and $\delta_x\zeta_n=n\zeta_{n-1}$ if $n>1$. The result \eqref{copy:shift} follows.
nodes.section: The $C^*$-algebra associated to expandable discrete analytic functions
nodes.statement_short: Apply $\delta_x$ to the generating function, which multiplies it by $z$, then read off the coefficients.

nodes.name: $\delta_y$ as a power series in $\delta_x$
nodes.statement: In $\cH_{DA}$ we have \[ \begin{split} \delta_y&=\delta_x\left(I-\frac{i-1}{2}\delta_x\right)^{-1}\\ &=\sum_{n=0}^\infty\left(\frac{i-1}{2}\right)^n\delta_x^{n+1}, \end{split} \] where the convergence of the above series is in the operator norm
nodes.section: The $C^*$-algebra associated to expandable discrete analytic functions
nodes.statement_short: In $\cH_{DA}$, $\delta_y=\delta_x(I-\frac{i-1}{2}\delta_x)^{-1}$, the series converging in operator norm.
conclusions: \[ \begin{split} \delta_y&=\delta_x\left(I-\frac{i-1}{2}\delta_x\right)^{-1}\\ &=\sum_{n=0}^\infty\left(\frac{i-1}{2}\right)^n\delta_x^{n+1}, \end{split} \] where the convergence of the above series is in the operator norm

nodes.name: Proof of the $\delta_y$ expansion
nodes.statement: Recall that the operator $\overline{\cD}$ was defined in \eqref{COP}. Since the elements of $\mathcal H_{DA}$ are discrete analytic we have $\overline{\cD}=0$ in $\mathcal H_{DA}$, that is, \[ (1-i)\delta_x+(1+i)\delta_y+\delta_x\delta_y=0, \] and thus \[ \delta_y\left((1+i)I+\delta_x\right)=(1-i)\delta_x. \] Since $\delta_x$ is an isometry, and has in particular norm $1$, we can solve equation \eqref{deltay1} and obtain \eqref{deltay}. The power expansion converges in the operator norm since \[ \|\left(\frac{i-1}{2}\right)\delta_x\|=\frac{1}{\sqrt2}<1. \]
nodes.section: The $C^*$-algebra associated to expandable discrete analytic functions
nodes.statement_short: Solve the discrete Cauchy-Riemann relation for $\delta_y$ and expand, using $\|\frac{i-1}{2}\delta_x\|=1/\sqrt2<1$.

nodes.name: The generated $C^*$-algebra is the Toeplitz algebra
nodes.statement: The $C^*$-algebra generated by $\delta_x$, or equivalently by $\delta_x$ and $\delta_y$ is the Toeplitz $C^*$-algebra.
nodes.section: The $C^*$-algebra associated to expandable discrete analytic functions
conclusions: The $C^*$-algebra generated by $\delta_x$, or equivalently by $\delta_x$ and $\delta_y$ is the Toeplitz $C^*$-algebra.

nodes.name: Proof that the algebra is Toeplitz
nodes.statement: This follows from the preceding proposition and from \cite{MR0213906}. Indeed it is known \cite{MR0213906} that the Toeplitz $C^*$-algebra $\mathcal T$ is the unique $C^*$-algebra generated by the shift. Since $\delta^*_x$ is a copy of the shift, and $\delta_y\in C^*(\delta^*_x)$, the result follows.
nodes.section: The $C^*$-algebra associated to expandable discrete analytic functions
nodes.statement_short: $\delta_x^*$ is a copy of the shift and $\delta_y\in C^*(\delta_x^*)$, so Coburn's uniqueness theorem applies.

nodes.name: The self-adjoint part $A={\rm Re}~\cZ$
nodes.statement: We now consider \[ A={\rm Re}~\cZ=\frac{1}{2}\left(\cZ+\cZ^*\right), \] where $\cZ$ is defined from Definition \ref{defmult}.
nodes.section: The $C^*$-algebra associated to expandable discrete analytic functions

nodes.name: Essential self-adjointness of $A$ and the induced semi-group
nodes.statement: \mbox{}\\ $(i)$ The operator $A$ is essentially self-adjoint on the linear span $\mathcal D$ of the functions $\zeta_n$, $n\in\mathbb Z_+$.\\ $(ii)$ On $\mathcal D$ it holds that \[ [\delta_x,A]=\frac{1}{2}\left(I+\delta_x+\delta_x^2\right). \] $(iii)$ There exists a strongly continuous one parameter semi-group $\alpha_t\,\,:\,\, \mathcal T\,\,\longrightarrow\,\, \mathcal T$ such that \[ (e^{itA})b(e^{-itA})=\alpha_t(b),\quad\forall t\in\mathbb R,\,\,\forall b\in \mathcal T, \] where $\mathcal T$ denotes the Toeplitz $C^*$-algebra.
nodes.section: The $C^*$-algebra associated to expandable discrete analytic functions
nodes.statement_short: $A$ is essentially self-adjoint on $\mathcal D$, has commutator $\frac12(I+\delta_x+\delta_x^2)$ with $\delta_x$, and $e^{itA}$ implements a one-parameter semi-group of the Toeplitz algebra.
conclusions: $(i)$ The operator $A$ is essentially self-adjoint on the linear span $\mathcal D$ of the functions $\zeta_n$, $n\in\mathbb Z_+$.
$(ii)$ On $\mathcal D$ it holds that \[ [\delta_x,A]=\frac{1}{2}\left(I+\delta_x+\delta_x^2\right). \]

$(iii)$ There exists a strongly continuous one parameter semi-group $\alpha_t\,\,:\,\, \mathcal T\,\,\longrightarrow\,\, \mathcal T$ such that \[ (e^{itA})b(e^{-itA})=\alpha_t(b),\quad\forall t\in\mathbb R,\,\,\forall b\in \mathcal T, \] where $\mathcal T$ denotes the Toeplitz $C^*$-algebra.

nodes.name: Proof of essential self-adjointness and the semi-group
nodes.statement: In $(iii)$, we denote by $e^{itA}$ the unitary one-parameter group generated by the self-adjoint operator $A$ from $(i)$. The matrix representation of $A$ with respect to the ONB $e_n:=\frac{1}{n!}\zeta_n$ is: \[ \begin{pmatrix} & & & & & & & &\\ & & & & 0 & & & &\\ & & &n-2&n-1&0& & &\\ & & &n-1&n-1&n&0& &\\ & & & &n &\boxed{n}&n+1&\\ & & & &0 &n+1&n+1&n+2\\ & & & &0&0&n+2&n+2\\ & & & & & &0&\\ \end{pmatrix} \] It is therefore a banded infinite matrix with terms going to infinity linearly with $n$. It follows from \cite{MR507913} that $A$ is essentially self-adjoint.\\ $(ii)$ By definition of $\cZ$ and $\delta_x$ \[ \begin{split} [A,\delta_x^*](e_n)&=(A\delta_x^*-\delta_x^*A)(e_n)\\ &=\frac{1}{2}(e_n+e_{n+1}+e_{n+2})\\ &=\frac{1}{2}(I+\delta_x^*+\delta_x^{*2})e_n, \end{split} \] and hence the result.\\ $(iii)$ We have \begin{equation} e^{itA}be^{-itA}=\sum_{n=0}^\infty \frac{(it)^n}{n!}\left({\rm ad}~A\right)^n (b), \end{equation} and \[ \left({\rm ad}~A\right)^{n+1} (b)=[A,\left({\rm ad}~A\right)^n b], \] We verify \eqref{sum} on monomials of $\delta_x$ and $\delta_x^*$ using \eqref{wert} and induction. See \cite{MR671318,MR548006} for more details regarding limits.
nodes.section: The $C^*$-algebra associated to expandable discrete analytic functions
nodes.statement_short: The matrix of $A$ in the ONB is banded with linearly growing entries, giving (i); (ii) is a direct commutator computation; (iii) follows by expanding $e^{itA}be^{-itA}$ in iterated commutators.

nodes.name: Pointer to flows
nodes.statement: The next corollary deals with a flow. For more information on this topic, see \cite{Nelson_flows}.
nodes.section: The $C^*$-algebra associated to expandable discrete analytic functions

nodes.name: The one-parameter group passes to a flow on the circle
nodes.statement: The one-parameter group $\left\{\alpha_t\right\}\subset{\rm Aut}~(\mathcal T)$ passes to a flow on the circle group $\mathbb T=\left\{z\in\mathbb C\,\,;\,\, |z|=1\right\}$.
nodes.section: The $C^*$-algebra associated to expandable discrete analytic functions
conclusions: The one-parameter group $\left\{\alpha_t\right\}\subset{\rm Aut}~(\mathcal T)$ passes to a flow on the circle group $\mathbb T=\left\{z\in\mathbb C\,\,;\,\, |z|=1\right\}$.

nodes.name: Proof that $\alpha_t$ descends to the circle
nodes.statement: By \cite{MR0213906}, the Toeplitz algebra $\mathcal T$ has a represnetation as a short exact sequence \[ 0\,\,\longrightarrow\,\,\mathcal T/\mathcal K\,\,\longrightarrow \mathcal T\,\,\longrightarrow\,\,C(\mathbb T)\,\,\longrightarrow\,\, 0, \] where $\mathcal K$ is a copy of the $C^*$-algebra of all compact operators on $\cH_{DA}$. Hence, \[ \mathcal T/\mathcal K\,\,\simeq\,\, C(\mathbb T). \] Since the left hand-side of \eqref{810} leaves $\mathcal K$ invariant, it follows that \[ \alpha_t\,\,:\,\,\mathcal T\,\,\longrightarrow\,\,\mathcal T \] passes to the quotient $\mathcal T/\mathcal K\,\,\simeq\,\, C(\mathbb T)$.
nodes.section: The $C^*$-algebra associated to expandable discrete analytic functions
nodes.statement_short: Use the Toeplitz extension $0\to\mathcal K\to\mathcal T\to C(\mathbb T)\to0$; $\alpha_t$ leaves $\mathcal K$ invariant so it descends.

nodes.name: Schur analysis and de Branges-Rovnyak spaces
nodes.statement: To set these results in a wider setting, let us recall a few facts on Schur analysis, that is, on the study of functions analytic and contractive in the open unit disk. If $s_0$ is such a function (in the sequel, we write $s_0\in\mathscr S$), the operator of multiplication by $s_0$ is a contraction from the Hardy space of the open unit disk $\mathbf H_2$ into itself. The kernel \[ \frac{1-s_0(z)s_0(w)^*}{1-zw^*} \] is then positive definite in the open unit $\mathbb D$, and its associated reproducing kernel Hilbert space $H(s_0)$ was first studied by de Branges and Rovnyak.
nodes.section: A reproducing kernel Hilbert space of entire functions
nodes.statement_short: Recalls the Schur class, the contractive multiplication operator on $\mathbf H_2$, and the positive kernel behind $H(s_0)$.

nodes.name: The operator $T$
nodes.statement: Thus, let $\cH$ be a Hilbert space, and let $\cO$ denote the space of $\mathbf L(\cH)$-valued functions analytic at the origin, and consider the linear operator $T$ on $\cO$ defined by \begin{equation} T(z^nA_n)=\dfrac{z^n}{n!}A_n,\quad A_n\in\mathbf L(\cH). \end{equation} Then $T\cO$ is a space of $\mathbf L(\cH)$-valued entire functions.
nodes.section: A reproducing kernel Hilbert space of entire functions
nodes.statement_short: $T$ divides the $n$-th Taylor coefficient by $n!$, carrying functions analytic at the origin to entire functions.

nodes.name: The $\prot$ product
nodes.statement: The operator $T$ induces a product $\prot$ of elements in $T\cO$ via $$(Tf)\prot(Tg)=T(fg).$$
nodes.section: A reproducing kernel Hilbert space of entire functions

nodes.name: $\prot$-inverse of $I_{\cH}-zA$ is $e^{zA}$
nodes.statement: Let $\cH$ be a Hilbert space and let $A$ is a bounded operator from $\cH$ into itself. Then the $\mathbf L(\cH)$-valued entire function $$(I_{\cH}-zA)^{-\prot}=(\sum_{n=0}^\infty\dfrac{ z^{n}A^n}{n!})=e^{zA}$$ satisfies \[ (I_{\cH}-zA)\prot (I_{\cH}-zA)^{-\prot}=I_{\cH}, \] and it is the only function in $T\cO$ with this property.
nodes.section: A reproducing kernel Hilbert space of entire functions
nodes.statement_short: The unique $\prot$-inverse of $I-zA$ in $T\cO$ is the exponential $e^{zA}$.
assumptions: Let $\cH$ be a Hilbert space and let $A$ is a bounded operator from $\cH$ into itself.
conclusions: Then the $\mathbf L(\cH)$-valued entire function $$(I_{\cH}-zA)^{-\prot}=(\sum_{n=0}^\infty\dfrac{ z^{n}A^n}{n!})=e^{zA}$$ satisfies \[ (I_{\cH}-zA)\prot (I_{\cH}-zA)^{-\prot}=I_{\cH}, \]
and it is the only function in $T\cO$ with this property.

nodes.name: Proof of the $\prot$-inverse formula
nodes.statement: This comes from the power expansion and norm estimates.
nodes.section: A reproducing kernel Hilbert space of entire functions
nodes.statement_short: Power expansion plus norm estimates.

nodes.name: The space $\bH$
nodes.statement: Take now $\cH=\mathbb C$ and let $\mathbf H_2$ denote the Hardy space of the unit disk. Then $T$ is a positive contractive injection from $\mathbf H_2$ into itself. Denote by $\bH$ the space $T\bH_2$ equipped with the range norm: $$\forall f\in\bH_2, \qquad \|Tf\|_\bH=\|f\|_2.$$ Then $T:\bH_2\longrightarrow \bH$ is unitary, and $\bH$ is a reproducing kernel Hilbert space of entire functions with the reproducing kernel $$K_{\bH}(z,w)=\sum_{n=0}^\infty\dfrac{(zw^*)^n}{(n!)^2}.$$
nodes.section: A reproducing kernel Hilbert space of entire functions
nodes.statement_short: $\bH=T\bH_2$ with the range norm is an RKHS of entire functions with kernel $\sum (zw^*)^n/(n!)^2$.
nodes.genus: a reproducing kernel Hilbert space of entire functions
differentia: the space $T\bH_2$ equipped with the range norm

nodes.name: Integral characterisation of $\bH$
nodes.statement: $\bH$ is the Hilbert space of entire functions such that $$\int_\CC|f(z)|^2K_0(2|z|)dA(z)<\infty,$$ where $$K_0(r)=\dfrac{1}{\pi}\int_\RR\exp(-r\cosh t)dt$$ is the modified Bessel function of the second kind of order $0$.
nodes.section: A reproducing kernel Hilbert space of entire functions
nodes.statement_short: $\bH$ consists of the entire functions square-integrable against the Bessel weight $K_0(2|z|)$.
assumptions: where $$K_0(r)=\dfrac{1}{\pi}\int_\RR\exp(-r\cosh t)dt$$ is the modified Bessel function of the second kind of order $0$.
conclusions: $\bH$ is the Hilbert space of entire functions such that $$\int_\CC|f(z)|^2K_0(2|z|)dA(z)<\infty,$$

nodes.name: Proof of the integral characterisation
nodes.statement: This follows from the fact that the Mellin transform of the square of the function $\Gamma$ is the function $K_0(2\sqrt{x})$. See for instance \cite[p. 50]{colombo} for the latter.
nodes.section: A reproducing kernel Hilbert space of entire functions
nodes.statement_short: The Mellin transform of $\Gamma^2$ is $K_0(2\sqrt{x})$.

nodes.name: $\bH$ is contractively included in the Fock space
nodes.statement: We note that $\bH$ is contractively included in the Fock space since the reproducing kernel of the latter is \[ K_F(z,w)=\sum_{n=0}^\infty \frac{z^nw^{*n}}{n!}, \] and \[ K_F(z,w)-K_{\bH}(z,w)=\sum_{n=0}^\infty(zw^*)^n\left( \frac{1}{n!}- \frac{1}{(n!)^2}\right) \] is positive definite in $\mathbb C$. See for instance \cite[Theorem I, p. 354]{aron}, \cite{saitoh} for differences of positive definite functions.
nodes.section: A reproducing kernel Hilbert space of entire functions
nodes.statement_short: $K_F-K_{\bH}$ is positive definite, so $\bH$ sits contractively inside the Fock space.

nodes.name: Pointwise multipliers of $\bH$ are constants
nodes.statement: In view of Liouville's theorem, the only multipliers on $\bH$ in the sense of the usual pointwise product are constants.
nodes.section: A reproducing kernel Hilbert space of entire functions
conclusions: the only multipliers on $\bH$ in the sense of the usual pointwise product are constants.

nodes.name: Contractive $\prot$-multipliers are $Ts_0$ with $s_0$ Schur
nodes.statement: A function $s\in\cO$ is a contractive $\prot$-multiplier on $\bH$ if and only if it is of the form $$s=Ts_0,\quad s_0\in\Sch,$$ where $\Sch$ denotes the Schur class of functions analytic and contractive in the open unit disk.
nodes.section: A reproducing kernel Hilbert space of entire functions
nodes.statement_short: The contractive $\prot$-multipliers on $\bH$ are exactly the images under $T$ of the Schur class.
assumptions: where $\Sch$ denotes the Schur class of functions analytic and contractive in the open unit disk.
conclusions: is a contractive $\prot$-multiplier on $\bH$ if and only if it is of the form $$s=Ts_0,\quad s_0\in\Sch,$$

nodes.name: Proof of the multiplier characterisation
nodes.statement: Assume first that $s\in\cO$ is a contractive $\prot$-multiplier on $\bH$. Then $s=s\lozenge1\in\bH$ and hence $s=Ts_0$ for some $s_0\in\bH_2$. Furthermore, let $f\in\bH_2$. Since $s\lozenge(Tf)=T(s_0f)\in\bH$, $s_0f\in\bH_2.$ Since $$\|f\|_{\bH_2}=\|Tf\|_\bH\geq\|s\lozenge(Tf)\|_\bH=\|T(s_0f)\|_\bH=\|s_0f\|_{\bH_2},$$ $s_0\in\Sch.$ Conversely, if $s=Ts_0$ where $s_0\in\Sch$, and $f\in\bH_2$ then $s\lozenge(Tf)=T(s_0f)\in\bH$ and $$\|s\lozenge(Tf)\|_\bH=\|T(s_0f)\|_\bH=\|s_0f\|_{\bH_2} \leq\|f\|_{\bH_2}=\|Tf\|_\bH.$$ Thus $s$ is a contractive $\prot$-multiplier on $\bH$.
nodes.section: A reproducing kernel Hilbert space of entire functions
nodes.statement_short: Transport the contraction inequality across the unitary $T:\bH_2\to\bH$ in both directions.

nodes.name: de Branges-Rovnyak space $H(s_0)$
nodes.statement: Let $s_0\in\mathscr S$. The operator $M_{s_0}$ of pointwise multiplication is a contraction from $\bH_2$ into itself. The operator range $\sqrt{I-M_{s_0}M_{s_0}^*}$ endowed with the range norm is called the associated de Branges-Rovnyak space. We denote it by $H(s_0)$.
nodes.section: A reproducing kernel Hilbert space of entire functions
nodes.genus: The operator range $\sqrt{I-M_{s_0}M_{s_0}^*}$ endowed with the range norm

nodes.name: The space $H(s)$
nodes.statement: Similarly one can associate with $s\in T\Sch$ a reproducing kernel $$K_s(z,w)=\left((I-M_sM_s^*)K_\bH(\cdot,w)\right)(z),$$ where $M_s$ denotes the operator of $\prot$-multiplication by $s$ on $\bH$. The corresponding reproducing kernel Hilbert space is $\ran(\sqrt{I-M_sM_s^*})$ with the range norm; it will be denoted by $H(s)$.
nodes.section: A reproducing kernel Hilbert space of entire functions
nodes.statement_short: $H(s)$ is the range of $\sqrt{I-M_sM_s^*}$ with the range norm, the $\prot$-analogue of $H(s_0)$.
nodes.genus: The corresponding reproducing kernel Hilbert space

nodes.name: $f\mapsto Tf$ is unitary from $H(s_0)$ onto $H(s)$
nodes.statement: The mapping $f\mapsto Tf$ is unitary from de Branges - Rovnyak space $H(s_0)$ onto $H(s)$.
nodes.section: A reproducing kernel Hilbert space of entire functions
conclusions: The mapping $f\mapsto Tf$ is unitary from de Branges - Rovnyak space $H(s_0)$ onto $H(s)$.

nodes.name: Proof of the unitary equivalence
nodes.statement: Since $$M_sT=TM_{s_0},$$ $$\sqrt{I-M_sM_s^*}T=T\sqrt{I-M_{s_0}M_{s_0}^*}.$$
nodes.section: A reproducing kernel Hilbert space of entire functions
nodes.statement_short: Intertwining passes to the defect operators.

nodes.name: The differentiation operator $\dd$
nodes.statement: The $H(s)$ spaces can be characterized in terms of $\dd$-invariance, where $\dd$ is the differentiation operator: $$\dd f = f^\prime.$$
nodes.section: A reproducing kernel Hilbert space of entire functions

nodes.name: Properties of $\dd$ on $\bH$
nodes.statement: The operator $\dd$ is bounded on $\bH$; moreover, \begin{equation} \dd T=TR_0, \end{equation} where $R_0$ is the backward shift operator, and $$\dd^*\dd=I_\bH-C^*C,\quad \dd\dd^*=I_\bH,$$ where $Cf:=f(0)$. Furthermore, the reproducing kernel of $\bH$ is given by $$K_\bH(z,w)=Ce^{z\dd}e^{w^*\dd^*}C^*.$$
nodes.section: A reproducing kernel Hilbert space of entire functions
nodes.statement_short: $\dd$ is bounded on $\bH$, intertwines with the backward shift via $T$, is a coisometry, and reproduces $K_\bH$.
assumptions: where $R_0$ is the backward shift operator
conclusions: The operator $\dd$ is bounded on $\bH$
\begin{equation} \dd T=TR_0, \end{equation}
$$\dd^*\dd=I_\bH-C^*C,\quad \dd\dd^*=I_\bH,$$
Furthermore, the reproducing kernel of $\bH$ is given by $$K_\bH(z,w)=Ce^{z\dd}e^{w^*\dd^*}C^*.$$

nodes.name: Proof of the properties of $\dd$
nodes.statement: The claims follow from the definition of the operator $T$ in \eqref{opeT}. We prove only \eqref{r0}. Let $f\in\mathbf H_2$ with power series expansion \[ f(z)=\sum_{n=0}^\infty a_nz^n. \] Then, \[ (R_0f)(z)=\sum_{n=1}^\infty a_nz^{n-1}, \] and therefore \[ \begin{split} (TR_0f)(z)&=\sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{a_n}{(n-1)!}z^{n-1}\\ &=\frac{d}{dz}\left(\sum_{n=0}^\infty \frac{a_n}{n!}z^n\right)\\ &=(\dd Tf)(z). \end{split} \]
nodes.section: A reproducing kernel Hilbert space of entire functions
nodes.statement_short: Compute $TR_0f$ termwise on power series and recognise it as $\dd Tf$.

nodes.name: $\dd$-invariant subspaces of $\bH$
nodes.statement: A closed subspace $H$ of $\bH$ is $\dd$-invariant if and only if $$H=\bH\ominus M_{Ts_0}\bH,$$ where $s_0(z)$ is an inner function.
nodes.section: A reproducing kernel Hilbert space of entire functions
nodes.statement_short: Closed $\dd$-invariant subspaces of $\bH$ are exactly the orthogonal complements of $M_{Ts_0}\bH$ for inner $s_0$.
conclusions: is $\dd$-invariant if and only if $$H=\bH\ominus M_{Ts_0}\bH,$$

nodes.name: Proof of the $\dd$-invariant subspace theorem
nodes.statement: Let $H$ be a closed subspace of $\bH$ then $H=TH_0$ where $H_0$ is a closed subspace of $\bH_2$. $H$ is $\dd$-invariant if and only if $H_0$ is $R_0$-invariant, which is equivalent to $\bH_2\ominus H_0$ being invariant under multiplication by $z$. By the Beurling-Lax theorem, the last condition holds if and only if $\bH_2\ominus H_0=M_{s_0}\bH_2,$ where $s_0$ is an inner function.
nodes.section: A reproducing kernel Hilbert space of entire functions
nodes.statement_short: Pull back to $\bH_2$ through $T$ and apply the Beurling-Lax theorem.

nodes.name: Realization of $s\in T\Sch$
nodes.statement: Let $s\in T\Sch$. Then $s$ admits the representation $$s(z)=D+\int_0^zCe^{t\dd}Bdt,$$ where $$\begin{pmatrix} \dd & B\\ C& D\end{pmatrix}:\begin{pmatrix} H(s)\\ \CC\end{pmatrix}\longrightarrow \begin{pmatrix} H(s)\\ \CC\end{pmatrix}$$ is a coisometry given by \[ \nonumber \begin{split} \dd f&=f^\prime,\\ B1&=s^\prime,\\ Cf&=f(0),\\ D1&=s(0). \end{split} \]
nodes.section: A reproducing kernel Hilbert space of entire functions
nodes.statement_short: Every $s\in T\Sch$ has an integral realization $D+\int_0^z Ce^{t\dd}B\,dt$ with a coisometric colligation.
conclusions: Then $s$ admits the representation $$s(z)=D+\int_0^zCe^{t\dd}Bdt,$$

where $$\begin{pmatrix} \dd & B\\ C& D\end{pmatrix}:\begin{pmatrix} H(s)\\ \CC\end{pmatrix}\longrightarrow \begin{pmatrix} H(s)\\ \CC\end{pmatrix}$$ is a coisometry given by \[ \nonumber \begin{split} \dd f&=f^\prime,\\ B1&=s^\prime,\\ Cf&=f(0),\\ D1&=s(0). \end{split} \]

nodes.name: Proof of the realization of $s\in T\Sch$
nodes.statement: Write $s=Ts_0$, where $s_0\in\Sch$. Then $$s_0(z)=D_0+zC_0(I-zR_0)^{-1}B_0,$$ where $$\begin{pmatrix} R_0 & B_0\\ C_0& D_0\end{pmatrix}:\begin{pmatrix} H(s_0)\\ \CC\end{pmatrix}\longrightarrow \begin{pmatrix} H(s_0)\\ \CC\end{pmatrix}$$ is a coisometry given by \[ \nonumber \begin{split} R_0 f&=(f-f(0))/z,\\ B_01&=R_0s_0,\\ C_0f&=f(0),\\ D_01&=s_0(0)=s(0). \end{split} \] Hence \[ \nonumber \begin{split} s(z)&=D_0+\sum_{n=0}^\infty \dfrac{z^{n+1}}{(n+1)!} C_0R_0^nB_0\\ &=D_0+\sum_{n=0}^\infty \dfrac{z^{n+1}}{(n+1)!}C_0T^{-1}(TR_0T^{-1})^nTB_0\\ &=D+\sum_{n=0}^\infty \dfrac{z^{n+1}}{(n+1)!}C\dd^nB\\ &= D+\int_0^zCe^{t\dd}Bdt. \end{split} \]
nodes.section: A reproducing kernel Hilbert space of entire functions
nodes.statement_short: Write $s=Ts_0$, use the classical backward-shift realization of $s_0$, and transport it by $T$.

nodes.name: Coisometric colligations give contractive $\prot$-multipliers
nodes.statement: Let $H$ be a Hilbert space and let $$\begin{pmatrix}A&B\\C&D\end{pmatrix}:\begin{pmatrix}H\\ \CC \end{pmatrix}\longrightarrow\begin{pmatrix}H\\ \CC\end{pmatrix}$$ be a coisometry. Then the function $$s(z)=D+\int_0^zCe^{tA}Bdt$$ is a contractive $\prot$-multiplier on $\bH$, and the corresponding reproducing kernel is given by $$K_s(z,w)=Ce^{zA}e^{w^*A^*}C^*.$$
nodes.section: A reproducing kernel Hilbert space of entire functions
nodes.statement_short: Any coisometry produces a contractive $\prot$-multiplier $s(z)=D+\int_0^zCe^{tA}B\,dt$ with kernel $Ce^{zA}e^{w^*A^*}C^*$.
assumptions: Let $H$ be a Hilbert space and let $$\begin{pmatrix}A&B\\C&D\end{pmatrix}:\begin{pmatrix}H\\ \CC \end{pmatrix}\longrightarrow\begin{pmatrix}H\\ \CC\end{pmatrix}$$ be a coisometry.
conclusions: Then the function $$s(z)=D+\int_0^zCe^{tA}Bdt$$ is a contractive $\prot$-multiplier on $\bH$
and the corresponding reproducing kernel is given by $$K_s(z,w)=Ce^{zA}e^{w^*A^*}C^*.$$

nodes.name: Proof that coisometries give $\prot$-multipliers
nodes.statement: Set $$s_0(z)=D+zC(I-zA)^{-1}B,$$ then $s_0\in\Sch$ and $s=Ts_0$. Since $$K_{s_0}(z,w)=C(I-zA)^{-1}(I-wA)^{-*}C^*,$$ the formula for $K_s(z,w)$ follows.
nodes.section: A reproducing kernel Hilbert space of entire functions
nodes.statement_short: Set $s_0(z)=D+zC(I-zA)^{-1}B\in\Sch$; then $s=Ts_0$ and the kernel formula follows from $K_{s_0}$.

nodes.name: Intrinsic characterisation of the $H(s)$ spaces
nodes.statement: A reproducing kernel Hilbert space $H$ of functions in $\cO$ is of the form $H=H(s)$ for some $s\in T\Sch$ if and only if \begin{enumerate} \item $H$ is $\dd$-invariant; \item for every $f\in H$ $$\|\dd f\|_H^2\leq\|f\|_H^2-|f(0)|^2.$$ \end{enumerate}
nodes.section: A reproducing kernel Hilbert space of entire functions
nodes.statement_short: An RKHS in $\cO$ is some $H(s)$ exactly when it is $\dd$-invariant and satisfies the defect inequality.
assumptions: A reproducing kernel Hilbert space $H$ of functions in $\cO$
conclusions: is of the form $H=H(s)$ for some $s\in T\Sch$ if and only if \begin{enumerate} \item $H$ is $\dd$-invariant; \item for every $f\in H$ $$\|\dd f\|_H^2\leq\|f\|_H^2-|f(0)|^2.$$ \end{enumerate}

nodes.name: Proof of the intrinsic characterisation
nodes.statement: One direction follows immediately from Theorem \ref{s2}. The proof of the other direction is modelled after the proof of \cite[Theorem 3.1.2, p. 85]{adrs} and is done as follows: let $H$ be $\dd$-invariant; then for every $f\in H$ $$Ce^{z\dd}f=f(z),$$ where $Cf=f(0).$ Hence the reproducing kernel of $H$ is given by $$L_(z,w)=Ce^{z\dd}e^{w^*\dd^*}C^*.$$ Since $$\dd^*\dd+C^*C\leq I,$$ there exists a coisometry $$\begin{pmatrix} \dd & B\\ C& D\end{pmatrix}:\begin{pmatrix} H\\ \CC\end{pmatrix}\longrightarrow \begin{pmatrix} H\\ \CC\end{pmatrix}.$$ But the the function $$s(z)=D+\int_0^zCe^{t\dd}Bdt$$ is a contractive $\prot$-multiplier and the associated kernel $K_s(z,w)$ coincides with $L(z,w)$. Hence $H=H(s).$
nodes.section: A reproducing kernel Hilbert space of entire functions
nodes.statement_short: One direction from the unitary equivalence; the other builds a coisometric colligation from the defect inequality, following de Branges-Rovnyak theory.

nodes.name: Towards $\prot$-rational matrix valued functions
nodes.statement: It is also of interest to consider $\prot$-rational matrix valued functions.
nodes.section: A reproducing kernel Hilbert space of entire functions

nodes.name: Characterisations of $\prot$-rationality
nodes.statement: Tne following are equivalent: \begin{enumerate} \item A function $f\in T\cO$ is $\prot$-rational in the sense that for some polynomial $p(z)$, not vanishing at the origin, $p\prot f$ is also a polynomial. \item $f(z)$ is of the form $$f(z)=D+\int_0^zCe^{tA}Bdt$$ with $A,B,C,D$ - matrices of suitable dimensions; \item the columns of $\dd f$ belong to a finite-dimensional $\dd$-invariant space. \end{enumerate}
nodes.section: A reproducing kernel Hilbert space of entire functions
nodes.statement_short: $\prot$-rationality, an $e^{tA}$ integral realization, and finite-dimensional $\dd$-invariance are equivalent.
conclusions: \item A function $f\in T\cO$ is $\prot$-rational in the sense that for some polynomial $p(z)$, not vanishing at the origin, $p\prot f$ is also a polynomial.
\item $f(z)$ is of the form $$f(z)=D+\int_0^zCe^{tA}Bdt$$ with $A,B,C,D$ - matrices of suitable dimensions;
\item the columns of $\dd f$ belong to a finite-dimensional $\dd$-invariant space.

nodes.name: Proof of the $\prot$-rationality equivalences
nodes.statement: It suffices to observe that a function $f\in T\cO$ is $\prot$- rational if and only if it is of the form $f=Tf_0$ where$f_0\in\cO$ is rational in the usual sense.
nodes.section: A reproducing kernel Hilbert space of entire functions
nodes.statement_short: $f\in T\cO$ is $\prot$-rational precisely when $f=Tf_0$ with $f_0$ rational in the usual sense.

nodes.name: The $\boxdot$ product
nodes.statement: In parallel with the previous section, we introduce the product $\boxdot$ of expandable discrete analytic functions by \[ \zeta_n\boxdot\zeta_m=\dfrac{m!n!\zeta_{m+n}}{(m+n)!}. \]
nodes.section: A reproducing kernel Hilbert space of expandable discrete analytic function
nodes.statement_short: The second product is defined on the basis by $\zeta_n\boxdot\zeta_m=m!n!\zeta_{m+n}/(m+n)!$.
nodes.definiendum: the product $\boxdot$ of expandable discrete analytic functions

nodes.name: Expandable functions form a ring under $\boxdot$
nodes.statement: The advantage of this product versus the C-K one is that the space of expandable discrete analytic functions forms a ring.
nodes.section: A reproducing kernel Hilbert space of expandable discrete analytic function
conclusions: the space of expandable discrete analytic functions forms a ring.
