nodes.name: The mapping $V$ and the identification $V\bH=\cH_{DA}$
nodes.statement: Consider the linear mapping $V:z^n\mapsto\zeta_n.$ Then $VT$ maps, in particular, the space of functions analytic in a neighborhood of the closed disk $\{z:|z|\leq1/\sqrt{2}\}$ onto the space of expandable functions. Then $V\bH$ with the range norm is the reproducing kernel Hilbert space $\cH_{DA}$ with the reproducing kernel \eqref{rkda} $$K((x_1,y_1),(x_2,y_2))= \sum_{n=0}^\infty\dfrac{\zeta_n(x_1,y_1)\zeta_n(x_2,y_2)^*}{(n!)^2}.$$
nodes.section: A reproducing kernel Hilbert space of expandable discrete analytic function
nodes.statement_short: $V:z^n\mapsto\zeta_n$ carries $\bH$ unitarily onto $\cH_{DA}$, and $VT$ onto the expandable functions.

nodes.name: Intertwining relations for $V$
nodes.statement: Note that $$V\dd=\delta_xV,\quad V(e^zA)=e_{x,y}(A).$$

nodes.statement_short: $V$ intertwines $\dd$ with $\delta_x$.

nodes.statement: A closed subspace $H$ of $\cH_{DA}$ is $\delta_x$-invariant if and only if $$H=\cH_{DA}\ominus M_{VTs_0}\cH_{DA},$$ where $s_0(z)$ is an inner function.

Then $s$ admits the representation $$s(x,y)=D+Ce_{x,y}(\delta_x)\boxdot (\zeta_1(x,y)B),$$ where $$\begin{pmatrix} \delta_x & B\\ C& D\end{pmatrix}: \begin{pmatrix} H(s)\\ \CC\end{pmatrix}\longrightarrow \begin{pmatrix} H(s)\\ \CC\end{pmatrix}$$ is a coisometry given by \[ \nonumber \begin{split} B1&=\delta_xs,\\ Cf&=f(0),\\ D1&=s(0). \end{split} \]

nodes.name: Coisometric colligations give contractive $\boxdot$-multipliers
nodes.statement: Let $H$ be a Hilbert space and let $$\begin{pmatrix}A&B\\C&D\end{pmatrix}:\begin{pmatrix}H\\ \CC \end{pmatrix}\longrightarrow \begin{pmatrix}H\\ \CC\end{pmatrix}$$ be a coisometry. nodes.name: Uniqueness of $\hat f$
nodes.statement: To show the uniqueness of $\hat f(n)$, assume that \eqref{tay} holds for some function $\hat f(n)$ and apply the identity \[\delta x^{[n]}=nx^{[n-1]}\] repeatedly to obtain \eqref{fou1}.
nodes.statement_short: Apply $\delta x^{[n]}=nx^{[n-1]}$ repeatedly to force the coefficient formula.
nodes.section: Polynomials and rational functions on the set of integers

nodes.name: Construct $\tilde f$ from the candidate coefficients
nodes.statement: Next, let the function $\hat f(n)$ be defined by \eqref{fou1}. Then, according to Proposition \ref{tay1}, the series $$\tilde f(x):=\sum_{n\in\ZZ_+} \hat f(n)x^{[n]}$$ converges absolutely for every $x\in\ZZ_+$ and defines a function $\tilde f:\ZZ_+\longrightarrow\CC.$ Hence \eqref{fou1} holds with $\tilde f$ replacing $f$ and $$\forall n\in\ZZ_+,\qquad (\delta^nf)(0)=n! \hat f(n)=(\delta^n\tilde f)(0).$$
nodes.statement_short: Define $\tilde f$ by the formula and match all differences at $0$.
nodes.section: Polynomials and rational functions on the set of integers

nodes.name: Induction on $x$
nodes.statement: Now one can verify that \[\forall x\in\ZZ_+,\,\,\forall n\in\ZZ_+,\qquad (\delta^nf)(x)=(\delta^n\tilde f)(x) \] by induction on $x$: If $$ \forall n\in\ZZ_+, \qquad (\delta^nf)(x)=(\delta^n\tilde f)(x)$$ then \begin{multline*} \forall n\in\ZZ_+, \qquad (\delta^nf)(x+1)=(\delta^nf)(x)+(\delta^{n+1}f)(x)\\= (\delta^n\tilde f)(x)+(\delta^{n+1}\tilde f)(x) =(\delta^n\tilde f)(x+1).\end{multline*}
nodes.statement_short: Propagate the equality of all differences from $x$ to $x+1$.
nodes.section: Polynomials and rational functions on the set of integers

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: It remains to set $n=0$ in \eqref{hu1} to obtain \eqref{tay}.
nodes.statement_short: Specialise to $n=0$ to recover the expansion.
nodes.section: Polynomials and rational functions on the set of integers

nodes.name: Recall the classical realization
nodes.statement: We first recall that a matrix-valued rational function of a complex variable can always be written in the form \[ r(z)=p(z)+C(zI-A)^{-1}B, \] where the matrix-valued polynomial $p$ takes care of the pole at infinity, and $A,B$ and $C$ are matrices of appropriate sizes. Furthermore, when the dimension of $A$ is minimal, the (finite) poles of $r$ coincide with the spectrum of $A$; see \cite{bgk1, MR0255260}. Here, we consider complex-valued functions, and thus $C$ and $B$ are respectively a row and column vector.
nodes.statement_short: Recall that a rational function of a complex variable is $p(z)+C(zI-A)^{-1}B$ with poles at $\sigma(A)$.
nodes.section: Polynomials and rational functions on the set of integers

nodes.name: Transfer to $\ZZ_+$
nodes.statement: Now, by Definition \ref{defrat1}, $f$ is a rational function if and only if it is the restriction on $\ZZ_+$ of a rational function of a complex variable, with no poles on $\ZZ_+$, that is if and only if it can be written as \eqref{eqreal} with the matrix $A$ satisfying furthermore \eqref{kaas}.
nodes.statement_short: Rationality on $\ZZ_+$ means being such a restriction with no poles on $\ZZ_+$.
nodes.section: Polynomials and rational functions on the set of integers

nodes.name: Expand in $y$ for fixed $x$
nodes.statement: First, fix $x\in\ZZ_+$ and consider the function $f_x:\ZZ_+\longrightarrow\CC$ given by $$f_x(y)=f(x,y),\quad y\in\ZZ_+.$$ Then, according to Proposition \ref{tay2}, there is a unique function $\hat{ f_x}:\ZZ_+\longrightarrow\CC$ such that $$\forall y\in\ZZ_+,\qquad f_x(y)=\sum_{n\in\ZZ_+}\hat{f_x}(n) y^{[n]};$$ the function $\hat{f_x}(n)$ is given by $$\hat{f_x}(n)=\dfrac{(\delta_y^n f)(x,0)}{n!},\quad n\in\ZZ_+.$$
nodes.statement_short: Apply the one-variable expansion in $y$ with $x$ frozen.

nodes.name: Expand the coefficients in $x$
nodes.statement: Next, fix $n\in\ZZ_+$ and consider the function $g_n:\ZZ_+\longrightarrow \CC$ given by $$g_n(x)=\hat{f_x}(n),\quad x\in\ZZ_+.$$ By the same Proposition \ref{tay2}, there is a unique function $\hat{g_n}:\ZZ_+\longrightarrow \CC$ such that $$\forall x\in\ZZ_+,\qquad g_n(x)=\sum_{m\in\ZZ_+}\hat{g_n}(m) x^{[m]};$$ the function $\hat{g_n}(m)$ is given by $$\hat{g_n}(m)=\dfrac{(\delta_x^m\delta_y^n f)(0,0)}{m!n!},\quad m\in\ZZ_+.$$
nodes.statement_short: Apply the one-variable expansion again to $g_n(x)=\hat{f_x}(n)$.

nodes.name: Combine the two expansions
nodes.statement: Thus $$\forall (x,y)\in\ZZ_+^2,\qquad f(x,y)=\sum_{(m,n) \in\ZZ_+^2}\hat{g_n}(m) x^{[m]}y^{[n]}.$$ It remains to set $\hat f(m,n)=\hat{g_n}(m).$
nodes.statement_short: Set $\hat f(m,n)=\hat{g_n}(m)$.

nodes.name: Finite support of $\hat f$
nodes.statement: First, in view of \eqref{fou11} and of the fact that $$\forall (m,n)\in\ZZ_+^2,\,\,\forall (x,y)\in\ZZ^2, \quad m+n>\deg(f)\Longrightarrow (\delta_x^m\delta_y^n f)(x,y)=0,$$ the function $\hat f$ has a finite support.
nodes.statement_short: High-order mixed differences of a polynomial vanish.

nodes.name: The expansion is the polynomial itself
nodes.statement: It follows that $$\sum_{(m,n)\in\ZZ_+^2}\hat f(m,n)x^{[m]}y^{[n]}$$ is, in fact, a polynomial, which coincides with the polynomial $f(x,y)$ on $\ZZ_+^2$ and hence on $\ZZ^2$.
nodes.statement_short: The finite expansion is a polynomial agreeing with $f$ on $\ZZ_+^2$, hence on $\ZZ^2$.

nodes.name: Build $h$ and check $\delta_x h=f$
nodes.statement: By Proposition \ref{p11}, there exist functions $\hat f,\hat g:\ZZ_+^2\longrightarrow\CC$ with finite support, such that $$f(x,y)=\sum_{(m,n)\in\ZZ_+^2}\hat{f}(m,n)x^{[m]}y^{[n]},\quad g(x,y)=\sum_{(m,n)\in\ZZ_+^2}\hat{g}(m,n)x^{[m]}y^{[n]}.$$ Then identity \eqref{co01} implies that \[\forall (m,n)\in\ZZ^2_+,\qquad (n+1)\hat{f}(m,n+1)=(m+1)\hat{g}(m+1,n).\] Consider the polynomial $$h(x,y)=\sum_{(m,n)\in\ZZ_+^2}\dfrac{\hat{f}(m,n)}{m+1} x^{[m+1]}y^{[n]}+\sum_{n\in\ZZ_+}\dfrac{\hat{g}(0,n)}{n+1}y^{[n+1]},$$ then $$\forall (x,y)\in\ZZ^2,\qquad(\delta_x h)(x,y)=\sum_{(m,n)\in\ZZ_+^2}\hat{f}(m,n) x^{[m]}y^{[n]}=f(x,y).$$
nodes.statement_short: Construct $h$ from the finitely supported coefficients of $f$.

nodes.name: Rewrite $h$ and check $\delta_y h=g$
nodes.statement: On the other hand, in view of \eqref{use03}, $$h(x,y)=\sum_{(m,n)\in\ZZ_+^2}\dfrac{\hat{g}(m,n)}{n+1} x^{[m]}y^{[n+1]}+\sum_{n\in\ZZ_+}\dfrac{\hat{f}(m,0)}{m+1}x^{[m+1]},$$ hence $$\forall (x,y)\in\ZZ^2,\qquad(\delta_y h)(x,y)=\sum_{(m,n)\in\ZZ_+^2}\hat{g}(m,n) x^{[m]}y^{[n]}=g(x,y).$$
nodes.statement_short: Use the compatibility relation to rewrite $h$ and obtain the second identity.

nodes.name: Minimal counterexample
nodes.statement: Assume the opposite, then $\deg(q)>0,$ and $q$ can be chosen so that $\deg q$ is the smallest possible.
nodes.statement_short: Assume a nonzero $q$ of least degree.

nodes.name: Both differences vanish
nodes.statement: Observe that $(\delta_xq)(x,y)$ is also a discrete analytic polynomial, that $ (\delta_xq)(x,0)\equiv 0,$ and that $\deg(\delta_xp)<\deg(p).$ Hence $(\delta_xq)(x,y)\equiv 0.$ Since $q(x,y)$ is discrete analytic, Definition \ref{maindef2} implies that $$\forall (x,y)\in\ZZ^2,\qquad (\delta_yq)(x,y)= \dfrac{i-1}{2}((1-i+\delta_y)\delta_xq)(x,y)= 0.$$
nodes.statement_short: Minimality kills $\delta_x q$, and discrete analyticity then kills $\delta_y q$.

nodes.name: Contradiction
nodes.statement: Thus $$(\delta_xq)(x,y)\equiv(\delta_yq)(x,y)\equiv 0$$ and hence $q=\const$ - a contradiction.
nodes.statement_short: $q$ is constant, contradicting $\deg q>0$.

nodes.name: Uniqueness from the lemma
nodes.statement: The uniqueness of the polynomial $q(x,y)$ follows from Lemma \ref{l1}.
nodes.statement_short: Cite the vanishing lemma.

nodes.name: Base case $p=\const$
nodes.statement: The existence in the case $p=\const$ is clear: it suffices to set $$q(x,y)=p(0).$$
nodes.statement_short: For constant $p$ take the constant extension.

nodes.name: Induction on $\deg p$
nodes.statement: If $p\not=\const$ we proceed by induction on $d=\deg(p)$. According to Proposition \ref{p03}, $(\delta p)(x)$ is a polynomial and $\deg(\delta p)=d-1$. Therefore, by the induction assumption, there is a discrete analytic polynomial $f(x,y)$, such that $$\forall x\in\ZZ,\qquad f(x,0)=(\delta p)(x)$$ and $\deg(f)=d-1.$ Let $g:\ZZ^2\longrightarrow\CC$ be defined by $$g(x,y)=if(x,y)-\dfrac{1-i}{2}(\delta_yf)(x,y),$$ then $g(x,y)$ is also a discrete analytic polynomial, $\deg(g)=d-1.$ Furthermore, since $(\bar Df)(x,y)\equiv 0,$ \begin{multline*}\forall (x,y)\in\ZZ^2,\quad (\delta_xg)(x,y)=i(\delta_xf)(x,y)-\dfrac{1-i}{2}(\delta_x\delta_yf)(x,y)\\= i(\delta_xf)(x,y)+\dfrac{1-i}{2}((1-i)(\delta_xf)(x,y)+(1+i)(\delta_yf)(x,y))= (\delta_yf)(x,y).\end{multline*} Hence, according to Proposition \ref{p13}, there exists a polynomial $h:\ZZ^2\longrightarrow\CC$ such that $$(\delta_xh)(x,y)\equiv f(x,y),\quad (\delta_y h)(x,y)\equiv g(x,y).$$ Since $$\forall (x,y)\in\ZZ^2,\qquad (\bar D h)(x,y)=(1-i)f(x,y)+(1+i)g(x,y)+(\delta_y f)(x,y)=0,$$ the polynomial $h(x,y)$ is discrete analytic.
nodes.statement_short: Extend $\delta p$ by induction, build $g$, then recover $h$ via the two-variable antiderivative.

nodes.name: Normalise $h$
nodes.statement: Finally, since $$\forall x\in\ZZ,\qquad (\delta_x h)(x,0)=f(x,0)=(\delta p)(x),$$ $h(x,0)-p(x)$ is a constant function. Thus it suffices to set $$q(x,y)=h(x,y)-h(0,0)+p(0)$$ to complete the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Shift $h$ by a constant so that it restricts to $p$.

nodes.name: Analyticity and Taylor coefficients $c_n$
nodes.statement: The analyticity is clear because $x,y\in\ZZ$ and we have $$e_{x,y}(z)=\sum_{n\in\ZZ_+}\dfrac{z^n c_n(x,y)}{n!},\quad \forall z\in\DD.$$ where $$c_n(x,y)=\dfrac{d^n}{dz^n}e_{x,y}\Bigm|_{z=0}.$$
nodes.statement_short: Introduce the Taylor coefficients $c_n(x,y)$ of $e_{x,y}$.

nodes.name: Difference recursion for $c_n$
nodes.statement: Since $$e_{x+1,y}(z)-e_{x,y}(z)=ze_{x,y}(z)=\sum_{n\in\ZZ_+}\dfrac{z^{n+1} c_{n}(x,y)}{n!},$$ $$\forall (x,y)\in\ZZ^2,\,\,\forall n\in\ZZ_+,\qquad (\delta_xc_{n})(x,y)=nc_{n-1}(x,y)$$ (if $n=0,$ $c_0(x,y)\equiv 1$ and $(\delta_xc_0)(x,y)\equiv 0$).
nodes.statement_short: $e_{x+1,y}-e_{x,y}=ze_{x,y}$ gives $\delta_x c_n=nc_{n-1}$.

nodes.name: The $c_n$ are discrete analytic
nodes.statement: Similarly, since \[ \begin{split} \dfrac{e_{x+1,y+1}(z)-e_{x,y}(z)}{1+ i}-\dfrac{e_{x+1,y}(z)-e_{x,y+1}(z)}{1-i}&=\\ &\hspace{-5cm}=\left( (1+z)\dfrac{1+i+iz}{1+i+z}-1\right)\dfrac{e_{x,y}(z)}{1+i}-\left( 1+z-\dfrac{1+i+iz}{1+i+z}\right)\dfrac{e_{x,y}(z)}{1-i}\\ &\hspace{-5cm}=0, \end{split} \] we have $$\forall (x,y)\in\ZZ^2,\,\,{\rm and}\,\,\forall n\in\ZZ_+,\qquad (\bar Dc_{n})(x,y)=0.$$ Thus, for every $n\in\ZZ_+$, the function $c_n:\ZZ^2\longrightarrow\CC$ is discrete analytic.
nodes.statement_short: The generating function satisfies the discrete CR equation, so each $c_n$ does.

nodes.name: Identify $c_n\equiv\zeta_n$ by induction
nodes.statement: Next, we show by induction that \[ \forall n\in\ZZ_+,\quad c_n(x,y)\equiv\zeta_n(x,y). \] Indeed, for $n=0$, $$c_0(x,y)\equiv 1\equiv\zeta_0(x,y).$$ Assume that, for some $n\in\ZZ_+$, $$c_n(x,y)\equiv\zeta_n(x,y),$$ then, in view of \eqref{hu3}, $$(\delta_xc_{n+1}(x,y)\equiv(n+1)c_n(x,y)\equiv (n+1)\zeta_n(x,y)\equiv(\delta_x\zeta_{n+1}(x,y),$$ hence $$(\delta_x(\zeta_{n+1}-c_{n+1}))(x,y)\equiv 0.$$ But the functions $c_{n+1}$ and $\zeta_{n+1}$ are discrete analytic, hence $$(\bar D(\zeta_{n+1}-c_{n+1}))(x,y)\equiv 0$$ and $$(\delta_y(\zeta_{n+1}-c_{n+1}))(x,y)\equiv 0.$$ It follows that $$\zeta_{n+1}-c_{n+1}=\const;$$ since $$\zeta_{n+1}(0,0)=0=c_{n+1}(0,0),$$ one concludes that $$c_{n+1}(x,y)\equiv\zeta_{n+1}(x,y),$$ and \eqref{hu4} follows.
nodes.statement_short: Both families satisfy the same recursion and vanish at the origin.

nodes.name: Part (1): restriction to $\ZZ_+$
nodes.statement: $(1)$ Setting $y=0$ in \eqref{ckdef} and taking into account the definition of $\cZ$ we have \[ \begin{split} (g\odot f)(x,0)&=c_0g(x,0)+c_1(\cZ g)(x,0)+\dots+c_n(\cZ^ng)(x,0)\\ &=c_0g(x,0)+c_1xg(x,0)+\cdots +c_nx^ng(x,0)\\ &=f(x,0)g(x,0). \end{split} \]
nodes.statement_short: Setting $y=0$ turns $\cZ$ into multiplication by $x$.

nodes.name: Part (2): uniqueness of the extension
nodes.statement: $(2)$ For an expandable function the discrete Cauchy-Riemann equation $\overline{D}f=0$ with prescribed initial values on the horizontal positive axis has a unique solution (see Theorem \ref{p52}).
nodes.statement_short: The discrete CR equation with prescribed axis values has a unique solution.

nodes.name: Part (3): commutativity
nodes.statement: $(3)$ is then clear from $(1)$ and $(2)$.
nodes.statement_short: Commutativity from (1) and (2).

nodes.name: Parts (1) and (2)
nodes.statement: The proofs of $(1)$ and $(2)$ are clear from the definition.
nodes.statement_short: Immediate from the definition of $\cZ$.

nodes.name: Part (3) via the commutator identity
nodes.statement: The proof of $(3)$ follows from the identity \eqref{id3} in Theorem \ref{tm34}.
nodes.statement_short: Preservation follows from the $[\overline{D},\cZ]$ identity.

nodes.name: Action of $\cZ$ on $\zeta_n$
nodes.statement: By Proposition \ref{ok}, for every $n\in\ZZ_+$, $(\cZ\zeta_n)(x,y)$ is a discrete analytic polynomial. In view of \eqref{xmult}, $$(\cZ\zeta_n)(x,0)= x\cdot x^{[n]}=x^{[n+1]}+n x^{[n]},$$ hence formula \eqref{hu5} follows from Theorem \ref{t1}.
nodes.statement_short: Compute $\cZ\zeta_n$ on the axis and lift by uniqueness of the extension.

nodes.name: Growth estimate survives
nodes.statement: Let $f_0:\ZZ_+\longrightarrow\CC$ be defined by \eqref{rest}, then $$(\cZ f)(x,0)= xf_0(x)=\sum_{n\in\ZZ_+}(n\hat{f_0}(n)+\hat{f_0}(n-1))x^{[n]},$$ where $\hat{f_0}(-1):=0.$ Since $$\limsup_{n\rightarrow\infty}(|\hat{f_0}(n)|n!)^{1/n}<\sqrt{2},$$ $$\limsup_{n\rightarrow\infty}(|n\hat{f_0}(n)+\hat{f_0}(n-1)|n!)^{1/n}<\sqrt{2}.$$
nodes.statement_short: The new coefficients $n\hat{f_0}(n)+\hat{f_0}(n-1)$ keep the $\sqrt{2}$ bound.

nodes.name: Assemble the expansion of $\cZ f$
nodes.statement: Finally, since $$f(x,y)=\sum_{n\in\ZZ_+}\hat{f_0}(n)\zeta_n(x,y),$$ where the convergence is absolute, $$(\cZ f)(x,y)=\sum_{n\in\ZZ_+}\hat{f_0}(n)(\cZ \zeta_n)(x,y)=\sum_{n\in\ZZ_+}(n\hat{f_0}(n)+\hat{f_0}(n-1))\zeta_n(x,y).$$
nodes.statement_short: Apply $\cZ$ termwise to the absolutely convergent $\zeta_n$-series.

nodes.name: Rational $\Rightarrow$ C-K quotient
nodes.statement: Suppose first that $f$ is rational, and let $f_0(x)$ denote the restriction of $f$ to the horizontal positive axis. By definition there exists two polynomials $p_0(x)$ and $q_0(x)$ such that $q_0(x)\not=0$ (on $\ZZ_+$) and \[ q_0(x)f_0(x)=p_0(x),\quad x\in\ZZ_+. \] Let $p(x,y)$ and $q(x,y)$ denote the discrete analytic polynomials extending $p_0(x)$ and $q_0(x)$ respectively. Then both $p$ and $q\odot f$ are expandable functions, which coincide on $\ZZ_+$, and therefore everywhere.
nodes.statement_short: Extend the numerator and denominator polynomials; they agree with $q\odot f$ on the axis.

nodes.name: C-K quotient $\Rightarrow$ rational
nodes.statement: Conversely, let $p(x,y)$ and $q(x,y)$ be the discrete analytic polynomials such that $$\forall x\in\ZZ_+,\qquad q(x,0)\not=0$$and $$(q\odot f)(x,y)\equiv p(x,y).$$ Setting $y=0$ leads to $$\forall x\in\ZZ_+,\quad q(x,0)f(x,0)=p(x,0),$$ which ends the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Set $y=0$ to exhibit $f(\cdot,0)$ as a quotient of polynomials.

nodes.name: Part (i): banded matrix gives essential self-adjointness
nodes.statement: In $(iii)$, we denote by $e^{itA}$ the unitary one-parameter group generated by the self-adjoint operator $A$ from $(i)$. The matrix representation of $A$ with respect to the ONB $e_n:=\frac{1}{n!}\zeta_n$ is: \[ \begin{pmatrix} & & & & & & & &\\ & & & & 0 & & & &\\ & & &n-2&n-1&0& & &\\ & & &n-1&n-1&n&0& &\\ & & & &n &\boxed{n}&n+1&\\ & & & &0 &n+1&n+1&n+2\\ & & & &0&0&n+2&n+2\\ & & & & & &0&\\ \end{pmatrix} \] It is therefore a banded infinite matrix with terms going to infinity linearly with $n$. It follows from \cite{MR507913} that $A$ is essentially self-adjoint.
nodes.statement_short: The matrix of $A$ in the ONB is banded with linearly growing entries.
nodes.section: The $C^*$-algebra associated to expandable discrete analytic functions

nodes.name: Part (ii): commutator computation
nodes.statement: $(ii)$ By definition of $\cZ$ and $\delta_x$ \[ \begin{split} [A,\delta_x^*](e_n)&=(A\delta_x^*-\delta_x^*A)(e_n)\\ &=\frac{1}{2}(e_n+e_{n+1}+e_{n+2})\\ &=\frac{1}{2}(I+\delta_x^*+\delta_x^{*2})e_n, \end{split} \] and hence the result.
nodes.statement_short: Compute $[A,\delta_x^*]e_n=\frac12(e_n+e_{n+1}+e_{n+2})$.
nodes.section: The $C^*$-algebra associated to expandable discrete analytic functions

nodes.name: Part (iii): the automorphism semi-group
nodes.statement: $(iii)$ We have \begin{equation} e^{itA}be^{-itA}=\sum_{n=0}^\infty \frac{(it)^n}{n!}\left({\rm ad}~A\right)^n (b), \end{equation} and \[ \left({\rm ad}~A\right)^{n+1} (b)=[A,\left({\rm ad}~A\right)^n b], \] We verify \eqref{sum} on monomials of $\delta_x$ and $\delta_x^*$ using \eqref{wert} and induction. See \cite{MR671318,MR548006} for more details regarding limits.
nodes.statement_short: Expand $e^{itA}be^{-itA}$ in iterated commutators and verify on monomials by induction.
nodes.section: The $C^*$-algebra associated to expandable discrete analytic functions

nodes.name: Necessity
nodes.statement: Assume first that $s\in\cO$ is a contractive $\prot$-multiplier on $\bH$. Then $s=s\lozenge1\in\bH$ and hence $s=Ts_0$ for some $s_0\in\bH_2$. Furthermore, let $f\in\bH_2$. Since $s\lozenge(Tf)=T(s_0f)\in\bH$, $s_0f\in\bH_2.$ Since $$\|f\|_{\bH_2}=\|Tf\|_\bH\geq\|s\lozenge(Tf)\|_\bH=\|T(s_0f)\|_\bH=\|s_0f\|_{\bH_2},$$ $s_0\in\Sch.$
nodes.statement_short: A contractive $\prot$-multiplier forces $s=Ts_0$ with $M_{s_0}$ contractive.
nodes.section: A reproducing kernel Hilbert space of entire functions

nodes.name: Sufficiency
nodes.statement: Conversely, if $s=Ts_0$ where $s_0\in\Sch$, and $f\in\bH_2$ then $s\lozenge(Tf)=T(s_0f)\in\bH$ and $$\|s\lozenge(Tf)\|_\bH=\|T(s_0f)\|_\bH=\|s_0f\|_{\bH_2} \leq\|f\|_{\bH_2}=\|Tf\|_\bH.$$ Thus $s$ is a contractive $\prot$-multiplier on $\bH$.
nodes.statement_short: Transport the Schur contraction estimate through the unitary $T$.
nodes.section: A reproducing kernel Hilbert space of entire functions

nodes.name: Easy direction
nodes.statement: One direction follows immediately from Theorem \ref{s2}.
nodes.statement_short: Cite the unitary equivalence.
nodes.section: A reproducing kernel Hilbert space of entire functions

nodes.name: Converse via a coisometric colligation
nodes.statement: The proof of the other direction is modelled after the proof of \cite[Theorem 3.1.2, p. 85]{adrs} and is done as follows: let $H$ be $\dd$-invariant; then for every $f\in H$ $$Ce^{z\dd}f=f(z),$$ where $Cf=f(0).$ Hence the reproducing kernel of $H$ is given by $$L_(z,w)=Ce^{z\dd}e^{w^*\dd^*}C^*.$$ Since $$\dd^*\dd+C^*C\leq I,$$ there exists a coisometry $$\begin{pmatrix} \dd & B\\ C& D\end{pmatrix}:\begin{pmatrix} H\\ \CC\end{pmatrix}\longrightarrow \begin{pmatrix} H\\ \CC\end{pmatrix}.$$ But the the function $$s(z)=D+\int_0^zCe^{t\dd}Bdt$$ is a contractive $\prot$-multiplier and the associated kernel $K_s(z,w)$ coincides with $L(z,w)$. Hence $H=H(s).$
nodes.statement_short: The defect inequality yields a coisometry whose associated kernel is the kernel of $H$.
nodes.section: A reproducing kernel Hilbert space of entire functions
